1 think this is the proper time for 'me to place before the committee a memorandum, and also a copy of a communication presented to 0ir Richard McBride when he was Prime Minister of British Columbia, concerning this proposed taxation on fuel oil. As I stated on a former occasion, we in Ontario are spending a good deal of money in order to get cheap power, while this Government is passing a Bill in order to make dearer power, which is now comparatively cheap. The memorandum reads: _
Some three or four years ago, due to the representations of the Government of British Columbia and the Board of Railway Commissioners, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company changed its locomotives running in certain districts from coal to oil burners. This change was made at the expense of $600,000, and was for the sole purpose of protecting the forests of British Columbia from fire.
The initial cost of crude oil to the company at that time exceeded the cost of coal, but some of this difference was absorbed by the certainty of the supply of oil and the uncertainty of the supply of coal as in the case of strikes, congestion, etc. The present tax on the amount imported for locomotives and steamship purposes shows the following result:
Proposed new taxation on 47,398,000 gallons, $236,992. Present taxation, $81,254.52; Increase, $155,737.48.
I give that as a sample of how the change effects the Canadian Pacific railway in making its motive power dearer. This company, like the Grand Trunk Pacific, I presume, at the suggestion of the Government of British Columbia and the Board of Railway Commissioners, changed its locomotives from coal burners to oil burners. This is the communication sent to Sir Richard McBride when he was Prime Minister of British Columbia:
Vancouver, B.C., 3rd March, 1915.
Hon. Sir Richard McBride,
Premier,
Victoria, B.C.	[DOT]
Dear Sir,-It has come to the knowledge of the large and important manufacturing interests, as well as the railway and steamship transportation companies operating in British Columbia, that your Government have recently been presented with a petition from certain parties interested in coal mining, urging your Government to support their application to the Federal Government for a duty on crude oil imported for fuel and manufacturing purposes. The undersigned, therefore, beg to respectfully urge that your Government do not support an application towards imposing a duty on crude oil for the above purposes, for the following reasons:
Until crude oil for fuel became available, manufacturing in British Columbia was practically at a standstill. Such industries as had been established, were being forced to close down or greatly reduce their operations, and new industries were deterred from establishing themselves, because of their inability to obtain suitable and sufficient coal to carry on their operations, and at a price that would make manufacturing possible. Steamship lines operating along the British Columbia coast, providing the necessary transportation facilities so important to the opening up of the mining, fishing and lumber industries, were unable to provide a satisfactory service because of their inability to obtain coal, and being in competition with oil burning steamers operating from Puget Sound, were placed at a great disadvantage, and Canadian interests were suffering. Railways were unable to handle * the increasing traffic to the satisfaction of the shipping and travelling public for the same reasons. This difficulty was largely owing to the numerous and frequently occurring labour disputes, which resulted in the closing of the mines. These disputes were not between Canadian employers and Canadian labour, but were forced upon the country by the dictation of union labour leaders in the United States. In the year 1911, the Canadian Pacific railway was placed in a position that compelled them, between the months of June

and December, to import from Pennsylvania over 32,000 tons of coal, and haul it from the head of the Great Lakes to the centre of this province, involving? a cost, over the price they would have paid for British Columbia coal, of $208,000. Again, in 1912, when another strike prevailed in the mines of Vancouver island, they had to import from the state of Washing- [DOT] ton about 40,000 tons of coal, at an expense of $154,000, although, at that time, they were! burning a large Quantity of fuel oil. That railway company found itself forced to go into the use of oil fuel for the reasons stated, although they realized that it would cost them $650,000 in order to use oil fuel, and spent that sum of money on its locomotives and steamers, and in providing the necessary equipment.
Immediately fuel oil became available, a great impetus was given to the establishment of manufactories of all kinds, and the opening up the full capacity of those already established. These included, among others, pulp and paper mills, cement manufactories, gas works, sugar refineries, and iron and steel works for .the fabrication and construction of tanks and other equipment; oil refineries, which, while they do not use oil for fuel have established important industries in the refining of this crude oil, a large percentage of the by-product, viz., " asphaltum," being in competition in Canadian markets with imported " asphaltum," which is,admitted free of duty, besides oils, distillates, etc. These, and numerous other industries, have been the means of giving employment to a large number of the highest class of labourers, and have enabled British Columbia manufacturers not only, to supply their own market, but to reach foreign markets, and this condition, we state in the most positive terms, could not have been accomplished had the manufacturing and transportation interests had to depend on British Columbia coal for fuel.
In respect to the railway operations. It is impossible to estimate the enormous saving that has accrued to the province of British Columbia through the use of fuel oil in certain districts, by reason of the elimination of the numerous devastating forest fires which were constantly occurring during the dry seasons, and which could not possibly be avoided in the operation of heavy grades with coal fuel. This has resulted in such an enormous saving to the lumber interests of the province at large, that the Commission on the Conservation of Forests have warmly commended those railways which have adopted oil fuel, and have urged that no other class of fuel be used through districts adjoining timber lands. In fact, the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada have issued an order that coal which throws sparks must not be used from April to October, which places a ban on a large proportion of coals of this province.
Many strong reasons could be advanced in support of our contention, but we would briefly reiterate our statement that the absolute inability of the coal mines, for reasons explained, to supply sufficient and suitable fuel, caused great delay to the development of the industries of the province, and consequent heavy loss; but the introduction of fuel oil, although it involved heavy expenditures on the part of the transportation and manufacturing interests, has enabled these industries to establish themselves, and although difficult, under present conditions, to. continue their operations, we submit that it would be not only an injustice but 
it would be fatal to the continuation of their' operations, should a duty such as suggested, be placed on this class of fuel, which is not, at present, produced in Western Canada. .
We desire to refer to the temporary war tax referred to in the budget by the hon. Minister of Finance, of 7} per cent on crude oil. ,
He is referring to last year's Budget.
The undersigned, in common with all other Canadian industries, stand ready to bear their share of the burden assumed by the Dominion of Canada, in its avowed policy of supporting the Empire in the defeat of the nation's enemies in the present war, and, therefore, if this tax is necessary for that purpose, we offer no protest, but gladly assume our share. At the same time, it might be pointed out that in view of the very large importation of crude oil into this province, necessary for the foregoing reasons, the war tax derived therefrom will, we believe, produce a larger revenue per capita from this province than from any other portion of the Dominion. We submit that the principle of the war tax is an equal distribution over the whole Dominion and we fear such will not be the result, for the reasons given. The undersigned, therefore respectfully request that you should place our views before the hon. Minister of Finance, so that should the demand of the coal mine interests go before the Federal Government, our views may receive their consideration :

I do not wish to take
up time at this stage, but a few words ought to be said as to this increase in the duty on apples. It is extremely unfortunate that, at this session, when the Government have sought to make Parliament and the country believe that they do not intend to deal with any contentious measure, but to confine attention chiefly to measures connected with the war, they should have introduced a proposal to increase the tariff upon an article of food so universally used by the people of Canada. The proposal is of a most controversial nature. It is in no way connected with the war, but has been introduced for the , declared purpose of encouraging the fruit-growing industry in British Columbia. It ought to be borne in mind that the three Prairie Provinces are not able to raise fruit. Fruit from outside their own boundaries is a necessity of life and not a luxury to the people there. It is very objectionable that at this time, when the people of the Prairie Provinces are bearing cheerfully their Share of the burdens which Canada is called upon to bear in connection with the war, an jincrease of taxation should be imposed upon an article so necessary for them. It is peculiarly unfortunate -that this should
be done at a time so closely following the action of the Congress of the United States in reducing the taxation upon this very article of food. Hon. members are no doubt aware that until 1914, that is until the Wilson tariff was enacted, the duty upon apples entering the United States was 25 cents per barrel, the Canadian duty being 40 cents per barrel. The Congress of the United States has reduced the tariff on apples from 25 cents to 10 cents per barrel, while now it is proposed by this Government to increase our tax from 40 cents to 90 cents per barrel. I should like to know what my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) thinks. My hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) when asked what the Minister of Trade and Commerce had said upon certain important matters, replied that he did not care. He is one of the young men on the Conservative side who have nq respect, apparently, for the opinion of -the elder statesmen of Canada. I can remember reading not many years ago an eloquent and forcible statement by the Minister of Trade -and Commerce addressed more particularly to the people of the United States on the subject of trade relations between the two countries, and in that speech or it may have been a magazine article -he said to the people of the United States: Lower your tariff wall, and you will find the people of Canada prepared, and joyfully prepared, to meet you.
But this Government is proposing to increase the duty on apples from 40 cents a barrel to 90 cents a barrel, thus making the Canadian duty on this most important article of food 900 per cent greater than the Lnited States tariff. This proposal is most objectionable, and extremely undesirable. It is placing in the hands of that section of the people- of the United States who would like to do away with the reduced tariff in respect of Canadian produce and get back to a high protective tariff the very weapon which they want and which they may use with good effect against Canadian produce in the not distant future. At the same time that the United States reduced the duty on apples, they reduced the duty on hay from $4 a ton to $2 a ton, under which vast quantities of Canadian hay have been sent into the United States, much to the advantage of the Canadian people. At the same time the United States Congress took off entirely the duty on lumber, and vast quantities of lumber have been sent into that country, where a market



of enormous importance for Canadian lumber is being found. Congress at the same time reduced the duty on oats from 15 cents a bushel to 6 cents a bushel, under which millions of dollars worth of Canadian oats find a ready and profitable market in the United States. In view of the fact that the United States have made these concessions to Canada in response to what has been thought to be the general desire of the public men and the people of Canada, is this the time for the Government to increase the duty on this important article of food and make it 900 per cent greater than the United States tariff on the same article? It is said that this action is necessary in order to prevent the ruin of the apple industry in British Columbia. Sir,
I do not believe it.' I believe that every skilled farmer in British Columbia engaged in the production of apples can compete against the importation of apples from the United States under a reasonable tariff. The fruit growers of British Columbia do not want and do not need a duty of 90 cents a barrel on apples. The proposed duty is altogether exorbitant, and altogether out of proportion to the cost of the production of this article of food. From the experience which I have had in travelling through that province, I know that the trouble with British Columbia arises through the booming methods which in recent years have been carried on there. Land suited only for mixed farming and ordinary agricultural purposes has been boosted and boomed as being adapted for fruit growing. Many big companies have bought out the farms, and have been the means of doing away with mixed farming and inducing the people to go into fruit growing upon land which is no more adapted for the growing of fruit than any of the agricultural lands in Eastern Canada. Ask the fruit growers of the Okanagan valley as to their experience last year, and they will all tell you that the experienced fruit growers made money out of the products of their orchards, and that they do not need this protection. They regard it as unreasonable and unfair to the rest of the people of Canada that this very high rate of taxation should be imposed on this most important article of food. I desire to protest in the strongest way possible against the action of the Government in regard to this duty. I say that it ought not to be imposed at any time, least of all at this time, when the Government is pretending to the people of this country that they desire not to introduce controversial mea-
sures, but to devote their attention to purposes connected with the successful carrying on of the war.

The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) made a statement that the experienced apple grower of British Columbia was quite satisfied, and was able to produce apples at a profit at the present-market. T.he hon. gentleman evidently is not aware that a delegation- of British Columbia fruit growers visited the Capital in the early days of the session, among whom were two of the largest and most experienced fruit growers in the province of British Columbia. The statement of the fruit growers of British Columbia is that they canpot produce apples at less than $1.08 per box, 3 boxes making a barrel, whereas last year they had to sell their apples at 80 cents per box. The hon. member from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) attributed some remarks to me which I did not use. I may look vary innocent, but I am not innocent enough to say, or to have said in this House, that the producer will not receive any more for Ihis fruit under the new conditions than he did under the old. What I did say was thait, the slaughtering of American fruit will be shut out of the prairie markets, the producer of British Columbia -would have a stable market in which to place bis- fruit; that he would be enabled thereby to get into closer touch with the actual consumer, and for that matter keep out the middleman, the net result being that the consumer would pay very little more for his apples, and the producer would get a greater price. As it is under present conditions, it i-s a well known fact that the producer in some of the western American states has over planted, he has more product than he can- take care of and get rid of in his logical market, and he has been making a slaughter market of our Prairie Provinces. Not only do they offer to the prairie market apples at a certain price in competition with other apples from British Columbia and
4 p.m. Ontario, but they send apples in there on consignment, and many consignments have brought less than the freight and duty. Apples have been sent to the Prairie Provinces for as low as 30 cents per box. Surely we must protect such an industry as the apple growing industry of this Dominion. It is certainly a growing industry, it is certainly an industry that is entitled to protection; and if we can get the market of Canada the other

things will follow, and the producer will get into close touch with the consumer. The consumer will pay very little, if any, more for his product. The producer will get the addition that is now eaten up by the middlemen owing to the fact that he can get quotations and consignments from the United States producers and thereby cut our product out of our own market.

I do not want to delay the committee for more than a minute, as I have already expressed my personal views on this alteration of the tariff; but I have had sent to me a copy of a letter written by a gentleman who has for some years been resident in British Columbia, which I think ought to be read for the benefit of the minister and of the committee. The letter gathers interest from the fact that it was sent to the Canadian Horticulturist in confirmation of views upon this subject which had apparently been expressed in that paper. The Canadian Horticulturist ought to know something about the growing of apples and about the effect of such a duty as this. Without further comment, I shall ask the committee to listen to this letter:
Dear Sir,-I have read with interest your editorial upon the increased duty on apples, and desire to express my belief in the correctness of your view that, while it will give some temporary relief to the growers of British Columbia, it will not be of permanent benefit. Not only will the financial benefits be capitalized upon the value of the land, but it will act as a hindrance to prevent the removal of the real handicaps which burden the development of all land property in that great province.
Our protective tariff policy imposed a greater burden upon the agricultural progress of British Columbia than upon that of our other provinces, owing to the expense of irrigation in the dry districts and the high cost of clearing the heavily-timbered lands of the coast and of other districts.
The high cost of living during the years of bringing the land under cultivation, and the necessity for intense cultivation of the available lands, has led largely to the growing of truck crops and of fruits, the perishable nature of which, from local points makes it a practical impossibility to obtain a fair return in the provincial or prairie markets open to them. Not only has this prevented profitable results, but the high tariff caused a special injury to the fruit industry: 1st, by encouraging the dishonest booming of land; 2nd, by leading growers in reckless planting of all kinds of fruit of almost every variety known, which too often was planted so close together that proper development was impossible, until one marvels at the folly and waste of a large part of the British Columbia orchards.
The high tariff was also used to bolster up the prohibitory railway and express rates which have so seriously militated against the well-being and progress of the province.
Two illustrations may make my argument clear:
CM". Green.]	.
The freight charge last year upon commercial fertilizers from Victoria to Summerland, on lake Okanagan, was $18 a ton, making the cost of superphosphate about $40 a ton, while here it was bought for $22 a ton, while ground rock phosphate from the state of Tennessee was delivered here by the carload at $9 per ton.
Grain from Calgary points to British Columbia buyers In the interior and at Vancouver was charged 19c. per bushei freight for a distance of 500 to 650 miles, while from Calgary to Fort William, 1,227 miles, the freight was but 13 3-10c. per bushel.
In such ways high tariff has worked to cause that province far greater losses than the extra price it brought to fruit growers could begin to pay for.
My conviction is that only after high tariffs are removed will the Pacific province fully come to its own. I believe that a fair competition with the Oregon and Washington growers would in the results be better for the fruit growers of British Columbia than protection, which in the end costs more than it benefits.
I am sure the minister will sympathize with a solitary free trader in this House in asking for a little information and in putting on record so much sound doctrine from a province where one did not expect to find it after having listened to the utterances of the members from that province. It would rather seem that in so far as tariff matters are concerned they will find a great deal more of it than they expect. If it surprises them, and causes them to change their attitude, so much better for them; if not so much the worse for them, but they can rely upon the fact that the sentiment is growing.

Coming from a portion of the country where we pay higher prices for fruit than are paid in any other part of Canada, I cannot allow this resolution, increasing the tariff on apples from 40 to 90 cents per barrel, to pass without uttering a word of protest. To give an illustration of some of the prices that we pay for apples in Regina, and at other places on the prairies: For No. 1 Northern Spies I have paid at Regina as high as $8 per barrel; for ordinarily good British Columbia apples the lowest price we paid last fall that I have personal knowledge was $1.90 or $2 per box, and these same prices apply to apples coming from Oregon and Washington. In my part of the country the average wage earner cannot afford to buy apples.
I am not sufficiently aware of the situation in British Columbia to express an opinion with regard to that province, but as far as the members from the prairie provinces are concerned, I do not believe they will be properly representing their

constituencies in this House if they support this increase in the duty on apples. The duty means that we shall have to pay more for every box and barrel of apples we buy in Western Canada. The hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Green), and other British Columbia members, say that so far as the apple growers in British Columbia are concerned the increase in d,uty will not mean an increased price to the consumer. If that is so, why in the name of common sense do they want an increase in duty? My opinion is, however, that just as soon as this increase in duty comes into force every consumer in the prairie provinces will have to pay an increased price on every box and barrel of apples he buys. If it costs $1-06 to produce the average box of apples in British Columbia, and we have to pay on an average $2.50 a box in Regina, the difference must go by way of illegitimate profit to some person. What that person is I do not know. I have never been able to figure it out. I remember years ago, when I lived in the province of Ontario, it was a common thing to buy apples for $1.50 or $2 a barrel in the orchards.
And in Nova Scotia.

Where does the difference go? Perhaps, the minister can tell us. It surely does not all go to the middleman. The point I wish to make is this-if this tariff will benefit any one at all it will benefit the fruit growers of British Columbia, and it is therefore simply another discrimination against the consumers of the prairie provinces. In the prairie provinces, unfortunately, we do not produce any fruit. But fruit is a very necessary article of food, and it is in the interests of a man's health that he should be able to get it. Thte duty, however, will only make it more difficult for men in my part of the country to get the fruit they desire to consume. I fail to see how the Minister of Finance can come to the conclusion that a duty of this kind is in the national interest. I have repeatedly heard him say that if such and such a thing were in the national interest he would put it on the statute book. He is apparently satisfied that to give more pro-.tection to a small class of the community in British Columbia is in the national interest. I am of the opinion that you cannot pick out any one item in the tariff and say that it is in the national interest. All tariffs are class legislation, and are passed for the benefit of a very few, at the cost of
the rest of the community. This increase in duty is simply another attempt, whether designedly or not, to throttle the people of the western provinces.
What is the percentage of American apples imported?

speechtext:
We imported
200.000	barrels.

I suppose there are in the three Prairie Provinces at least
1.500.000	consumers of apples. I agree with the hon. member for Regina that it is good for people to eat apples, but my experience is that the people in the western provinces do not eat apples to the extent they did when they lived in an apple-growing country.
Does the hon. gentleman mean that they have not got the habit of eating apples?

I say, that as a fact, they have not the habit to the extent they had when they lived in parts of the country where apples were cheaper. I, of course, believe my hon. friend when he says he paid $8 a (barrel for Northern Spies. I would not suggest that he was exaggerating, but I am afraid that he was taken in.

I have never paid less than $6.
Mr. (SCHAFFNER:	The difference in
price of Ontario apples at Brandon and Regina should not 'be very much. In my town, the price of Ontario winter apples, such as Northern Spies, Greenings, Russets, etc., ranges from $3.75 to $5 a barrell. The apple question has been before t'he Agricultural Committee, of which I am a member, a great many times. I have often heard it said in the committee, that the apples in Ontario are not worth picking, and are left on the trees. I do not think I am far out when I say that apple growers in Ontario consider $1.50 a barrel a good price for the fruit as it stands in the orchard.
Not last year.

I think that is a good average price and if that is so, there is no reason why the people of Regina should have to pay $8 a barrel for the same fruit. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) mentioned the middlemen, and I should like to ask him a question on that point; I ask it entirely for information. The hon. member attributed the high pric*

of fruit largely to the middlemen. That has been the case in the past, and it is perhaps true to a certain extent to-day. Speaking of >my own district, I know that in Boissevain, the so-called middleman has very little opportunity of selling apples or any other fruit, foT practically all the Ontario fruit used by the prairie consumers is brought in by the grain growers. The grain growers can bring in winter apples from Ontario, and perhaps from Nova Nova Scotia, at from $3.75 to $4 a barrel. I think this is one of the ways in which the grain growers have been useful to the consumers on the prairies. It has always seemed to me that the high price is not attributable to the middleman. I think that freight and express rates have a great deal to do with the cost of apples, in my part of the country at all events. In my district we use very few American apples; what we do import are almost entirely early apples ripe in the month of September. As soon as the fruit grown in the east has matured, ninety per cent of out total consumption, if not more, comes from Ontario. If a certain article can be produced in Ontario at a Certain figure, and the people of the West have to pay a great deal more for that article, it seems to me it would be a splendid occupation for any Government that happened to be in power to ascertain the reason for the difference in price. The people of the Western Provinces are willing to pay their full sfiare of taxation, whether war or ordinary taxation, but on this question of apples-and I am by no means a free trader; with the light I have, it seems almost useless to be talking about free trade in a country like ours-I am bound to say that I most heartily sympathize with the idea that the duty on apples should not be increased, for it will mean an increased price to consumers in the Prairie Provinces.
The hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Green) said, on the authority of an association of apple growers in British Columbia, that it cost $1.06 a box to produce apples in that province.
As a matter of fact, it is $1.08.

Now, the apple growers received last year 80 cents a box. That means there is a difference of 28 cents between the selling price of the apples, and tlhe price they can produce them at. Apples were higher last year than the year before;

I think it is generally conceded that the British Columbia grower got a better price for apples last year than he had been getting for many years previous. He got 80 cents a box, and there was a duty, of 20 cents a box.
The duty was about 15 cents.

The duty is 40 cents a barrel until this new tax comes into effect; then there is a 7J per cent ad valorem duty, which brings the total duty to about 20 cents a box. The increase the minister proposes is an increase from 20 cents to 30 cents a box; that is, an increase of 10 cents a box. This duty, we are told, is to save the apple industry of British Columbia. But let us see. The British Columbia grower got 80 cents a box last year. The increase the Minister of Finance proposes works out, at the most to 10 cents a box, and that gives 90 cents a box on last year's price, which is still 18 cents a box less than the hon. member for Kootenay says the apples can be profitably produced for. Therefore there is no salvation for the industry in this proposition. As a matter of coming to the assistance of the apple growers of British Columbia, it may have merit, but to save the apple industry of British Columbia, it has absolutely' no merit, on the statement that my hon. friend has made. Let me make this suggestion first of all in line with what has been said by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. W. M. Martin) and the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner). The high cost of apples in the prairie provinces has kept down the consumption of apples there. The lower the price the greater the consumption, and the higher the price the less the consumption. What the producer of British Columbia wants is an ample market at his door. If the price of apples is such as to keep down the consumption, then he has not the market. If the price of apples is kept down, then the market is there for him to get. There are other and better ways of affecting the cost of apples to the consumer and the price to the producer than by a readjustment of the tariff. The freight on a box of apples, weighing fifty pounds gross, from Salmon Arm to Edmonton, 525 miles by rail, is 38 cents; the freight on a barrel of apples, equal, to three boxes, from Ontario to Edmonton is $1.95, which would make the proportional freight on a box 65 cents.
Is that by the carload or by the single barrel?

By the carload. 65 cents a box is the proportionate rate from Ontario to Edmonton as compared with 38 cents a box from Salmon Arm to Edmonton; that is 65 cents for hauling 50 pounds of apples 2,200 miles and 38 cents for hauling the same weight of apples 525 miles. Therefore the rate from Salmon Arm to Edmonton is four times, per mile What it is from Ontario to Edmonton. If we cut the rate from Salmon Arm to Edmonton to the same basis as the Ontario rate, the former rate would be about 17 cents a box as against 38 at the present time. I submit that a readjustment of the freight rates would be an elementary proposition looking to the expansion of the apple industry of British Columbia by cheapening the cost of apples to the prairie consumer and thereby enabling the British Columbia producer to get some part of the difference. Supposing that they were able to split between them the difference in the freight rate, it would be to their mutual advantage and it would double the advantage to the producer, because it would widen his market by reducing the price.
There is no argument in regard to extortion in the distribution of apples. Those who have control of the apple trade simply take advantage of their situation to levy an unjust toll upon the consumer and unduly to depress the price to the producer, and the higher the tariff is the more effectually can they do that work. My hon. friend, says that by this increase in the tariff the British Columbia producer is going to be protected against apples imported from Washington being slaughtered on the western market. Apples, he says, are being slaughtered on the western market to-day with a protective duty of 20 cents a box.

My hon. friend is wrong as to that. The duty is not over fifteen cents or seventeen cents at the outside. When you ad,d the percentage for the straight duty it is from fifteen to seventeen eents, an average of about fifteen cents.

The straight duty of forty cents a barrel will be thirteen and a third cents per box. The seven and a half per cent ad valorem duty added to that will, I maintain, und,er the very drastic conditions imposed by the Customs Department, bring the duty up to approximately twenty cents a box. The hon. Solicitor General, when he was addressing the House on this subject.
explained that that was how the duty figured out; in fact, he made it worse than that, because, he said, as Hansard will show, that the additional duty now being proposed was adding, not thirty cents, but only twenty-five cents a barrel. The exact amount of the duty, however, depends on the actual figures calculated by the Customs Department, with which figures, of course, we are not acquainted, but it is a fair proposition to say that the protective duty on a box of apples will be twenty cents, and in the face of that protection apples were slaughtered, they say, in the western provinces. If that were the case with a protective duty of twenty cents a box, will they not be slaughtered equally with a protective duty of ten cents a box more? The producer declared that he needed to get 26 cents a. box more to make his business a paying proposition. He surely expects to get the full benefit of the ten cents a box increased duty, and if he gets it, that is all the protection he has against the slaughtering of apples from Washington; and, if he does not get it, he has not even that much protection against that slaughtering of apples. It is a truism to say that the men, who control the market to-day under present conditions by reason, in large measure, of the tariff which now exists, will be able proportionately to increase their control with the increase in that tariff, and that instead of the tariff working to the benefit of the apple producer of British Columbia, it will work to his injury, because he will be that much tighter in the grip of the combine that handles the apples. That is my contention in regard to the matter and I respectfully submit it to the consideration of the Minister of Finance. This is a far-reaching and very important question. The Minister of Finance in some of his remarks saw fit to minimize it and so did the Solicitor General in some of his remarks, but it is a most important question in fact and in principle. We, in Alberta, are interested in the development of the orchards of British Columbia, naturally expecting to get some benefit' from that development, just as the people who produce the apples expect to derive some advantage from the development of the farms in the Prairie West. But if the middleman stands straddling the Rocky Mountains and robs them with one hand and us with the other, we are of no benefit to them and they are of no benefit to us. That is the point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman speaks of the middleman straddling the Rocky Mountains and taking a profit from the residents of the Prairie Provinces and also from the fruit growers of British Columbia. As I followed his argument, it seems to me it would apply in all matters of tariff. If he is logical-and he assumes to be, and I think likes to be logical -then his argument means that the mines of Nova Scotia derive no advantage from the duty on coal. Let him test that theory by the good sense of the people of Nova Scotia. I invite him to go with the member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) to that hon. gentleman's constituency, and promulgate that doctrine there. I do not believe he will find it received with great favour, or that it will carry the popular judgment. According to the hon. gentleman's argument the steel industries of Canada are not in the least degree benefited by the tariff which protects them from dumping by American producers. But I think he will meet very hostile opinions if he puts that view before the steel manufacturers of Canada, who ought to know their own business best.
I hope the committee will not think I am discourteous if, in view of the very full discussion which took place upon the resolutions, I do not go over the same ground again. But there have been questions as to cost of production, and when there is a dispute upon a question of that kind, it always seems to me advisable to call in an impartial witness, an expert who can have no object in misleading the House or the country. I will quote again what I quoted when the resolutions were in committee, an extract from the report of Mr. D. Johnson, the Fruit Commissioner, with regard to this matter of the cost of production in British Columbia and the price the fruit grower there was able to obtain for his product. It seems to me that Mr. Johnson might be looked upon as an impartial expert witness. He said:
It has been shown at the Experimental Station that it costs $1.08 per box, equal to $3.24 per barrel, to produce apples in British Columbia, yet the average price (f.o.t>.) obtained for this fruit in 1914 was 80J cents per box, equal to $2.41 per barrel.	*
That is to say, in the opinion of the fruit commissioners, there was a loss to the fruit growers of British Columbia of 27i cents a box, or 83 cents a barrel, though some hon. gentlemen opposite seem to think that the fruit growers of British Columbia are mak-

ing money on their industry. There is another report to which I call attention, that of Mr. Flack who is Chief Fruit Inspector for the Dominion. He ought to be an impartial expert witness. He says:
Many Washington growers are unable to continue with the low prices realized for their fruit. Foreclosures, I was informed, were quite common. It has often been asked me, " How is it that the Washington growers can sell so cheaply and make money and the British Columbia growers cannot? " My observations were that the Washington grower is not making money and cannot survive the low prices. The British Columbia situation reminds me of a merchant endeavouring to compete with a bankrupt stock.
This shows the character of the competition to which the British Columbia fruitgrower has been exposed, by reason of the abnormal situation existing in the northwestern states of the American Union. The producers there have a large market in their own country, where their better grades of fruit can be disposed of to good advantage, while their lower grades are shipped away, to be sold at such prices as they may be able to obtain. My hon. friend from Regina has questioned my statement that this matter was of national importance. As I said in committee, it would seem to me that anything that concerns agriculture-and fruit-growing is a part of agriculture-is of national importance. And, in order that the committee may know that this matter is not purely one local to British Columbia, I desire to read for the information of the committee an extract from the report of the Fruit Growers' Association of Ontario, held in Toronto, January 18-20 last. Ontario, we all know, is one of the principal, if not the principal, fruitgrowing province in Canada:
A new and very serious situation now faces the men who have, at large expense, established extensive orchard holdings throughout the province, i.e., the enormous and what is considered unfair competition of the surplus fruit of foreign countries in our own markets during the fruit season. This competition is considered unfair and destructive for several reasons, of which the following might be mentioned:
The fruit areas in the United States are very extensive, and, owing to climatic conditions, many of them are able to ripen and put their fruits on the market a few days to several weeks in advance of similar varieties of the home grown product. These fruits are put on our markets at the height of the shipping season, often at very low prices, with the result that when the home grown fruit appears the consuming public has already been largely supplied with fruits of these kinds, and a very poor market is the result for the Canadian producer. At times serious over-production occurs in the American fruit districts, and, in order to save their own markets, heavy supplies of surplus fruit are dumped on the Canadian market and

sold for what they will bring, causing complete demoralization of the fruit market for the time being.
With regard to the importation of apples, there are two important phases to the trade worthy of notice. These importations consist of two classes or grades: first, a limited importation of extra fancy or fancy fruit, and, second, very large consignments of "C" or third grade western apples. These latter are consigned more particularly to the markets of our Northwest provinces.
In regard to the former class of fruit, this is sold chiefly to restaurants and fruit stands, which are largely controlled or owned by foreign dealers, whose habits of life are distinct from those of British or Canadian born, and who reap large profits owing to their methods of living and to the sale of these fruits in small lots at fancy prices.
An increase of duty on this fruit would not be seriously felt by the consumer, but would largely come out of the profits of the foreign dealers.
With reference to the latter grade, as before stated, immense shipments of this class of fruit finds its way into the consuming centres of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and is frequently sold to the wholesale trade at below cost of production in order to relieve the American market, thus supplanting the legitimate market of Canadian producers both from the eastern provinces and British Columbia.
It is felt that this competition is unfair and destructive, and not particularly in the interests of the western consumer, from the fact that with a little encouragement home grown fruit can be supplied in sufficient quantities and at reasonable prices to amply supply this section of Canada from the provinces previously mentioned.	>
It appears to me that, as Canada is an agricultural country, it is a national policy, a proper policy, to protect the products of agriculture if they need protection. Do they need protection where, as in the apple industry, they are exposed to a competition from the United States, whose apple growers have a market for their better grades and so can sell at much below their cost of production their inferior grades by dumping in this market? Is that fair to the agriculturists of this country? I believe in protection, I believe in protection for the agriculturists of this country as much as for the manufacturers of this country. I claim to know something about the sentiment in agricultural Ontario, and many agriculturists of that province, and, I believe, many agriculturists in the eastern provinces generally, and I believe many agriculturists in the Prairie Provinces, as well as the fruit growers of British Columbia, are in favour of a reasonable degree of protection to Canadian agriculture. This Bill will inure to the benefit not only of the fruit growers of British Columbia, but of every farmer in the province of Ontario, every farmer in the province of Quebec, every farmer in the Maritime Provinces.
It will inure also, if apples can be raised in the Nort'h-West, to the ultimate advantage of the Northwest itself, because I believe that industry can be encouraged, whether agricultural or otherwise, by a proper tariff. I rose merely for the purpose of bringing these expert opinions to the attention of the committee and of showing how this matter is Regarded by the fruit growers of Ontario and by the farming' community of that province as well. The result of this tariff will be this: I do not say that it will shut out American fruit wholly-I do not think that desirable-but it will have a tendency to prevent the slaughtering of apples in Canada by American fruit growers at prices 'below the cost of production. I do not believe that the people of Canada desire to buy the products of our agriculturists at less than the cost of production to the farmers. I think if that were put fairly to the people of any community, in Canada they would say: we want to pay at least the cost of production to the agriculturists, and we are willing to pay a little more, because we would like to see our fellow-citizens get a reasonable profit upon their industry. I am not at all afraid that this is going to have a serious effect on the consumer of the West. It will tend to give a larger market in the West to the fruit growers of British Columbia. It will also have the tendency, so far as the whole of Canada is concerned, to promote the great fruit growing industry, which is capable of indefinite expansion. What is the reason why a community which is, and I hope always will be, practicallly agricultural, cannot raise all the fruit that is required by its inhabitants?' Is there any reason why Canada should have to look to another country for fruit?' Our climatic conditions are such that we can compete with any country in the world. I believe that our apples are of a better flavour and quality than apples grown to the South. Should we not so arrange our fiscal policy that the farmers and fruit growers of this country should be able to supply the consumers with such fruit as they require? That does not mean that fruit growers will take a toll from the consumers, because in this country, so largely agricultural, we shall have the benefit of competition; the farmers and fruit growers all over this country will be competing one with the other in the markets of Canada. No one will suggest a combine among all the farmers and all the fruit growers in this country to maintain a

high price against the consuming public. That is the safeguard against oppression or injustice to the consumer-the competition -which will result of the agriculturists all over this country in the production of *agricultural products and of fruit. This legislation is designed to save the agricultural community and the fruit-growing community from a competition, which, on the lace of it, is manifestly unfair to them, and which would ultimately have the effect of destroying, or at least severely injuring, their industry.

Just a word in connection with the hon. minister's reference to the report of Mr. Johnson. In view of the fact that he gives the average cost of producing a barrel of apples in British Columbia as $3.24, I think we should have a statement as to why it costs so much more to grow apples in British Columbia than it does to grow them in other parts of the Dominion. I am sure that $3.24 a barrel is much beyond the cost of producing apples in Eastern Canada.
Sir THOMAS WHITE-. Mr. Johnson states that it has been shown at the Experimental 'Station that it costs. $1.08 a box, equal to $3.24 a barrel, to produce apples in British Columbia.
Why does it cost so much more in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that for some years past the fruit growers of British Columbia have been conducting their business at a loss. One reason for that is that the planting has greatly increased in

British Columbia. In 1911 there was in British Columbia 1,976,425 trees, and in 1913, 2,291,173 trees. There has been an increase in production from 210,000 boxes in 1910, to 787,750 boxes in 1915. The number of carloads in 1910 was 350 and in 1915, 1,313. W'hile planting has been on the increase in British Columbia, and while new trees have been continually coming into bearing, in Washington and Oregon there has been over-planting and over-production. The result is that the British Columbia fruit grower, the number of whose trees has been increasing, and whose pro- . duct has been multiplied four-fold in five years, finds himself in competition with the greatly over-produced 'situation in the United States, and in competition, as one of the experts of the Agricultural Department has put it, of a .character similar to that which a merchant experiences in competition with a bankrupt stock.

It seems to me from the report of Mr. Johnson that it costs $3.24 *to produce a barrel of apples in British Columbia is a Teason why the duty on apples should not be increased at the present time. If it costs $3.24 to produce a barrel of apples, we cannot hope by any duty that we can put on to put the grower of British Columbia in a position to grow apples successfully. I have been making some in-' quiiy as to the cost of apples-not having reference to the Northern Spy and one or two of the better grades. My. information is that the apple grower of Ontario does not receive an average price of one dollar per barrel for his apples at the orchard. It costs probably $1 per barrel for picking the apples, packing them and hauling them from the orchard to the railway station, so that when the minister imposes a duty of 90 cents a barrel on apples, he is putting on a duty of from 75 per cent to 100 per cent on the cost of the apples at the orchard. I ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance if it is reasonable to impose a duty of practically 100 per cent? If our friends growing apples in British Columbia need a duty of from 75 per cent to 100 per cent on apples, is it fair to the balance of the people of Canada, the great consuming classes of Canada, that this industry should ,be protected to such an extent? You might as well say that we could grow oranges and lemons in Canada. You could grow them under glass, and if you put the duty high enough and prohibited .the importation of other oranges and

lemons, we could probably produce some, but it would be at a great loss. Why should the people of the whole of Canada practically be made to pay extra prices when it has been shown very clearly this afternoon that, even with the duty that is being put on, you cannot hope to protect the industry in British Columbia to an extent that will make it profitable, according to the figures delivered by the Minister of Finance. I ask the Minister of Finance if he will not soften his heart and listen to the plea of the farmers from the Prairie Provinces who will pay this increased burden. Will he not listen to the plea of the hon. member for Cape Breton, and let the baby in the western provinces have its apple at the old price?

We had this matter
of the increased duty on apples before us some few days ago, and I had hoped that, in the meantime, additional information would have been brought down to the House as to the principles upon which the proposed increase is made. I wish to emphasize	the point	made by my hon.
friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) that the	Government has given us very
little information indeed.	The
only statistics which we have before us are the conclusions of a Mr. Johnson, an inspector of the Department of Agriculture, who shows, according to the figures quoted by the minister this afternoon, that there is a loss in growing British Columbia apples of over 80 cents a barrel. The proposal of the minister is to increase the duties by 30 cents a barrel. It is quite evident that there will still be a loss of 50 cents a barrel, which the minister has not provided for, and which causes one to ask on what principle the increase of duties is based. I could understand the minister trying to make up the loss and saying that he would give them .a chance to come out even, toy endeavouring to provide for the 80 cents. I-eould understand that he might say: Well, we will let the people of British Columbia do as the people of Saskatoon have to: If they make unprofitable investments they may have to let them go to tax sale. I could understand that, because that is what we are having to do. But I cannot understand on what basis the minister arrives at the conclusion that am increase of 30 cents a toanrel is going to make up a loss of 80 cents a barrel. Surely, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), other elements enter into the price
which is obtained by the grower of British Columbia, or in fact of any other part of the country, such as the relation of freights to cost of growing, the elements of marketing. I should like to know from the minister whether he has conducted any inquiry along those lines, so that by reducing the expenses of marketing or of growing or of freights, that loss could toe overcome, rather than by additional taxation. My hon. friend from Souris pointed out what is absolutely correct, that the western farmers are willing indeed to endure their share of the burden of raising the revenues of the country. This, however, is not a duty which will raise revenue; it is a purely protective tariff. It is an increase which will probably bring about a loss in revenue, so that the proposed duty will result im an increased price to the farmer through taxation which it is intended to hand over to the fruit-grower of British Columbia. Then, too, the prairie farmer must share in any deficit which
5 p.m. is brought about by decreasing the importation from cutside. I would simply ask my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to reconsider this item, to let it stand and get more information. 1 had hoped that he might come to the conclusion that there were other methods of benefiting the apple producers of British Columbia than the imposition of this increased duty.
I understood from the figures which the minister read that it costs $3.21 a barrel to produce apples in British Columbia. Does that mean in the orchard, or packed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Packed, produced, ready for shipment.

It has been said by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House that inferior apples from the state of Washington are slaughtered on the prairie markets, and that it is that slaughtering at low prices that prevents producers in British Columbia from making profits. As a matter of fact, in the city of Edmonton, Washington apples are sold, I shall not say in preference to British Columbia, but they are sold on the same counter, for the same price, on their merits; and it is a very great question if, on the average, the quality of the Washington fruit is not superior to that of British Columbia fruit. I do not wish to make any comparisons; but I wish to place that statement of fact before this House, as showing that the conditions indicated by

hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House are exaggerated, so far as the experience of one who lives right in that country and buys those apples would indit cate.
As far as the price is concerned, I verily believe that the apple dealers' combine buys these apples in Washington and Oregon, at low priees. I do not know whether they do or not-I presume they do-but they do not sell them to the consumers of Alberta at low prices. They get exactly the same price for the same quality of goods whether they come from British Columbia or from the state of Washington. Therefore, the idea that has been put forward on the other side of the House that the trouble with the British Columbia fruit growers is that inferior Washington and Oregon fruit is slaughtered in the Canadian market is simply an error; that is not the market condition at all.
The minister has given his statement to the House. He has not questioned the figures I have given as to freight rates or as to the proper and fair cost of boxes and distribution. He has given us no suggestion as to any reduction in these intermediary charges which are really what is the matter with both the consumer and producer of apples, in the Prairie Provinces and in British Columbia. Assuming that it cost $1.08 to produce a box of apples in British Columbia and that the intermediary charges are 80 cents, out of which there will be 38 cents freight, which is exorbitant and almost double what it should be compared with the rate on apples from Ontario, we should be able to buy apples in Alberta at $1.88 a box, giving the producer his full price, giving fair charges for carriage and distribution we should be able to buy our apples at $1.88 instead of paying $2.25 for apples for which the producers only get 80 cents. I do not think there is any argument proving that the fact that the tariff being low is what is wrong with the apple industry, and an increase of the tariff to an amount of 10 cents a box is not going to save the situation. It will make it worse for the producer as well as for the consumer, because it gives that much more liberty to the apple combine to depress prices at one end and increase them at the other.
Bill reported.

No. 67, relating to St. Peters Indian reserve.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
With reference to Bill No. 67 entitled, "An Act relating to the St. Peters Indian Reserve," the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), on Thursday last, when the resolution on which the Bill is founded was reported to the House, raised the question as to whether this was not a measure that required the consent of the Crown before proceeding further. The Bill was allowed its first reading and a second reading ordered for a future day on the understanding that I would consider this point in the meantime and give a ruling upon it.
Upon looking into the authorities on the subject, I find that where the consent of the Crown is required it may be announced by a minister at any stage of the Bill in question, in this respect differing from that class of bills where a preliminary recommendation of the Crown is necessary. The consent of the Crown is required when property rights of the Crown are postponed, compromised or abandoned, or where some prerogative of the Crown is to be waived. See May (Ilth edition) pp. 448, 561; also Bourinot (3rd edition) pp. 576, 578, and notes.
In the Bill under consideration it appears that certain grants made to the Crown by virtue of statutes in force at the time are confirmed. This confirmation does not, in my view upon a study of the authorities, require any additional consent of the Crown to Ihat already presumably furnished when the statutes were passed. The present Bill, however, appears to grant in addition to a confirmation of title, power to the Government to release liens held and liabilities due or to become due by virtue of the enactment. In this aspect of the case, I am of the opinion that the measure would require that the consent of the Crown be announced to the House at some stage of the Bill before its*final passage.
The subject matter of the Bill has been submitted to His Excellency the Governor General, who has consented to the same.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
On section 2-patents confirmed:

I should like some information as to the effect of these subsections. I see that subsection (a) provides

that the lands still held by the Indians are to be patented without any further consideration, and that subsection (b) provides that where the lands have passed out of the hands of the Indians, the sum of one dollar per acre, with five per cent interest per annum, is to be paid as a condition of the patent being confirmed. A patent was issued by the Dominion Government to the purchasers of these lands. Has the Government cancelled that patent?
No.

The course of events was that the registrar of land titles for Manitoba, acting under the Manitoba legislation, refused to register the patent which had been issued by the Dominion Government. Until the patent was registered under the laws of that province, the land could not be legally transferred. Is that the case?
Yes.

So the refusal of the registrar to register the title had the effect, not of depriving the purchaser of his property, tout of creating the property a non-negotiable .asset; that is, the purchaser's ownership in the property remained absolutely as it was before, tout he was prevented from selling it. Of course, the refusal to register had the effect of prejudicing the value of the property, .and to that extent deprived the purchaser of the advantage he hoped to gain by the purchase of the property. Now, this patent was issued, and has not been cancelled. For what reason is it believed that the registrar of land titles in Manitoba would [DOT] now refuse to register these titles, irrespective of the legislation now proposed ?

Before the registrar would undertake to pass favourably upon the titles, he made the request that either the Superintendent 'General of Indian Affairs, or the Solicitor General, or some other officer representing the Department of Justice, should guarantee that at the present session of Parliament legislation would be introduced, and if possible passed, confirming the patents. I, as Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, stipulated last fall that such legislation would be introduced this session, and from that time on the registrar has been passing favourably upon the titlesi

I think I understand the situation, tout I should like to have it made
perfectly clear. This legislation is not mandatory, either as regards the registration of these titles, or as compelling the registrar for Manitoba to refrain from registering until this legislation is passed and complied with.

The hon. gentleman has stated the case very fairly. He knows why the registrar would not pass favourably upon the titles: Doubt was cast upon the titles owing to the surrender having been declared invalid, and there was the report of tlhe commission. The Government do not at all recede from the position they took some years ago, that it was not a valid surrender, but still maintain that view. But it was decided that it would be best in the interests of all parties-it would avoid the delay that court proceedings would entail, and would give the purchasers clear title to the lands, and allow the district around Selkirk to develop-if we enacted the legislation asked for by the registrar of land titles for Manitoba.

The action entered by this Government in the Exchequer Court was * an action attacking the validity of the title which the previous Government had issued. That action has been entered, and prosecuted to some degree, I presume. Is that .action to be withdrawn as a result of this legislation toeing introduced?

If any purchaser of these lands does- not desire to avail himself of this legislation, he is still at liberty to prosecute his own case. The action has not been withdrawn from the Exchequer Court. Those Who wish to avail themselves of this legislation, by paying an aditional one dollar for the registration of title, can have their title favourably passed upon. Those who do not wish to do so need not do so.

I hope the minister will
pardon me for pursuing these inquiries so very strongly, but I merely wish to have the matter on record that we may understand it properly. This Government entered suit in the Exchequer Court to invalidate the titles that had been issued to this property. Is that action to be continued or is it to be withdrawn?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I would say that it will be continued as to any who do i.ot come in under this settlement. There may be none who will decline to come in under the settlement, and in that case the action will be at an end. If there are some who decline to come in, the action will continue.
2,'il8

Then the effect is hardly as it was previously presented to the House. It is a fact that this Government is still pressing its attack upon the validity of the titles issued by the previous Government, and will continue to press that attack until the purchasers pay one dollar additional per acre.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The balance of the litigation, i;f -any, will apply to sudh lands as belong to those who refuse to pay. As to pressing the action, I do not know if there will be any pressing of a defendant who refuses to come in. He himself, of course, will want the suit to be disposed of, and the suit will go on; and our side of the litigation will be upheld, at all events until the matter gets to the court. The balance of the litigation will not affect at all any lands the title to which is validated by this legislation.

I quite understand, but what I wanted to get straight was this: as I understood the case as presented by my hon. friend and by the Minister of Justice, further legal proceedings would be taken on the initiative of the purchaser^ of the land in maintaining their titles; but, as a matter, of fact, proceedings have been taken by the Government to invalidate the titles, and those proceedings will stand and be pressed unless and until the purchasers pay up the additional dollar per acre. That is really the situation. What I want to have on record is that this Government is continuing its action against these purchasers ; it is not the purchaser who has to take action against the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the purchaser is satisfied with his title as it is, I presume he will defend it and not settle. This legislation confirms the title of every one who chooses to avail himself of it and make' settlement.
. Our action against anybody who does that necessarily falls because that man's title is confirmed, even assuming that we -were perfectly right in our contention. As regards the others, the status quo is theirs, action having been taken. I presume, if a man does not want to settle, he will want to go on and have the question determined, because he will not want to hold property with this doubt cast upon his title to it. In any event, in the case of those who do not want to settle, the action is standing against them, and I do not see why it should not be proceeded with in the interest of both parties to the litigation.
[Mr Meighen.]
That is what I want demonstrated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am sorry if any misapprehension has been created. I certainly had no intention the other day to cause any, and I think the Solicitor General and myself said that it was optional to the parties holding the property to avail themselves of this legislation or not, just as they thought best.
I understood it was optional to the parties whether or not they should press a case on their own behalf against the Government in connection with the granting of the titles.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did not mean to convey that impression.

The matter is a complicated one and I merely want to get it as straight as possible on the record. This Government having entered action to invalidate those titles now decides that on the payment of an additional dollar an acre, they will withdraw their action so far as those lands are concerned, tout it will stand so far as the other lands are concerned. That, however, has no effect, whatever, except by understanding, upon the action of the registrar, Which after all is the essential point in the matter. This legislation does not presume to control or direct and it could neither control nor direct the registrar of Manitoba. As I understand the matter, he is at liberty to register or not register as he pleases, whether this legislation is passed or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I presume, of course, he would act rationally; he would not refuse to register on a mere arbitrary ground. As' 1 understand the situation, the registrar refused because there was at all events a doubt as to the validity of the title. This , legislation will remove that doubt so far as those are concerned who avail themselves of it, and I should assume that, when the reason which moved the registrar to refuse to register disappears, he will no longer refuse to register. He is not, however, an officer of this Government, and is not under its control.

I desire to have this
thoroughly understood, that this legislation neither controls nor directs the actions of the registrar of Manitoba, and that it is upon the action that he takes that these people depend for their right to transfer their property, and not upon this legisla-

tion. I do not wish, to enter into a controversy in regard to this matter and I do not want to discuss the motives of the registrar of Manitoba. I will, however, take the liberty of putting this point before the committee. Assuming that the registrar of the Land Titles Office in Manitoba refused to register because he believed that the Indians had been illegally and improperly deprived of valuable rights in that land to anything like the amount that had been stated upon the responsibility of members in this House, when he finds that this Government introduces legislation, which is not necessary at all and which is not effective in any way except as a noth fication that a certain action that the Government entered has been withdrawn, conditioned upon the payment of an additional one dollar an acre by those men who bought land from the Indians, if he were an honest man, which I may isay I do not think he is, or if he were moved by honest motives, which I do not believe-I take the *liberty of saying .so here-I would say that as an honest man he would be compelled by the action that is taken by this Government under this legislation to register all the titles presented to him for legislation, on the purchase price agreed upon in tho.se titles having been paid.
