On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), Bill No. 68, relating to the Superior Courts of Saskatchewan and to amend the Judges Act was read the second time, and the. House went into committee thereon, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
On section 1-Salaries of Judges of Superior Courts of Saskatchewan:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
May I ask
some explanation of paragraph a:
The Chief Justice of Saskatchewan, if he is also the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal, and if not to the Chief Justice of Appeal, $8,000.
I infer from this that there are two chief justices, the Chief Justice of Saskatchewan, and the Chief Justice of Appeal. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. There is at present a chief justice of Saskatchewan. There is only one Supreme Court in Saskatchewan, and the appeals go to the full bench of
judges of the Supreme Court, and the chief justice of the court is at present the Chief Justice of Saskatchewan. He was appointed Chief Justice of Saskatchewan, and it is not proposed to deprive him of the office. He may be appointed to be Chief Justice of Appeal; he may not. The purpose of making the distinction is that we want to give the salary of $8,000 to the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal. It will go to the present Chief Justice of Saskatchewan should he be appointed to the position of Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal. Should he not be so appointed the $8,000 salary will go to the gentleman who is appointed Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The chief justice will have the title and nothing more.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps there is not very serious Teason to apprehend that he will be without right to the title. He might be chief justice of the new Court of King's Bench and. retain his title as Chief Justice of Saskatchewan. But he would not, because of 'his title of Chief Justice of Saskatchewan, have the salary of $8,000. The intention is to attach the salary of $8,000 to the chief justiceship of the Court of Appeal.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: After the law of the province comes into force there will be a chief justice of Saskatchewan and a chief justice of the Court of Appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It might so happen, unless we do something to alter the commission of the present Chief Justice of Saskatchewan. I do not think there is very serious ground to apprehend that.
Is this legislation in consequence of a statute passed by the Legislature of Saskatchewan ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; we should not have the power to pass this Bill if they had not constituted these new courts.
Is there a separate court of appeal in Alberta? *

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, the court in Alberia is similar to the court in Saskatchewan to-day. They have a Supreme Court of Alberta, and appeals go from the judge to the court en .banc, composed, I think, of three judges of the court.

Although what I am going to say does not apply to tlhe courts of Saskatchewan, I think it is germane to the present Bill. I wish to speak about the number of judges in the province of

Quebec. My hon. friend (Mr. Doherty;, who for many years sat on the Bench at Montreal and who made a distinguished reputation for himself there, must have observed that there were complaints on the part of members of the Bar, the board of. trade, la ehambre de commerce, manufacturers and business men, on account of the delays, which are indeed too many, in cases brought before the courts. I have in mind just now a protest to which much prominence has been given of late, made by Hon. Mr. Amyot, who is a leading manufacturer in the city of Quebec, and a member of the Legislative Council. He has a large business which extends beyond the bounds of Canada. He said that the judicial system as it was organized in Montreal-even as it had been reorganized- did not meet with the approval of the public; that business men were discouraged; that something should be done by both the Provincial Government and by the Federal Government, to improve the situation; that cases which had been before the courts for a year, or even two years, had not been heard; and he thought the time had come when there should be a change in the judicial system of the province of Quebec. Hon, Mr. Amyot only voiced the feelings of a great dumber of people. It is true there are some districts of the province of Quebec in which the judges have very little to do. The business seems to be concentrated in the city of Montreal, and also partially in the cities of Quebec, Three Rivers, and Sherbrooke. I have some statistics on. the subject, but I will not weary the House by reading them. One can assert that more than half,' and perhaps three-quarters, of the judicial business of the province of *Quebec, is centered in Montreal; I have forgotten the number of judges whose residence is at Montreal, but perhaps my hon. friend the Minister of Justice can tell me. ^t all events, their number is certainly inadequate to the business, which is increasing year by year. The Minister of Justice listened to public opinion two years ago and increased the number of judges of the circuit court. And, although he increased their number by only one, yet that increase proved a real benefit to the litigants in that district. Besides, my hon. friend was good enough to specially appoint some judges of the Superior Court to. take up the arrears, so as to bring to a. hearing the cases which were pending. 3 must say that his plan worked very sue-fMr. Lemieux.]
cessfully. What I would suggest is that my hon. friend during the parliamentary recess take up this question with the Attorney General and the Bar of the province of Quebec with a view to seeing whether or not reorganization of the system in that province could be effected along the lines of the Ontario plan. In the province of Ontario the judges of the high court, rather than being domiciled in rural districts in the province, are centered in Toronto, and from Toronto they go to every district in the province. That system has worked most satisfactorily. Although I do not practise in Ontario, I have the honour of being a member of the Ontario bar, and I have often discussed this matter with members of the bar. I have been surprised to see that in this great province there is no complaint as regards the management of the laTge amount of judicial business that is carried on. Cases are heard and judgments rendered with practically no delay. We do not hear in the province of Ontario the complaints that we hear in the province of Quebec, where, for reasons well known, the litigants are face to face from the beginning of the year to the end, with the same person as judge in one district. I quite understand that when our judicial system was established before confederation by Sir George Etienne .Cartier, that system was really the proper one. Railways did not then extend their lines all over the province and give easy communication to the travelling public, and it was impossible to have the judge domiciled at the shire town or chef-lieu of the county or district. But to-day things are quite different. You can travel from one end of the province to the other within a few hours. You can send the judge from Montreal to the most distant district-even the district of Gaspe-and have him return within a few hours after he has finished his work. It seems to me that in view of the growing business in the larger districts, the judges from the rural districts should be brought to Montreal, where they would have the benefit, first, of an excellent library; second, of the advice and opinion of their brother judges, and, third, of sufficient business to occupy their attention from the beginning of the year to the end. In some districts the judge works perhaps only four or five days during the month; in other districts the judge may work during even a lesser period. Why should not these judges be called to Montreal and there help their, brother judges to

expedite business? But, as these judges are not obliged to go to Montreal, they may always find an excuse for disregarding the appeal that may be made to them-although I do not say that this happens, or that it has happened. Some years ago the present Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain), then Attorney General for the province of Quebec, had a Bill prepared with a view to reorganizing the whole system upon the same plan as that which is followed in the province of Ontario. I had a copy of that Bill, but unfortunately it was destroyed in the fire; my hon. friend will remember the principal features of it. At that time there were some prejudices against that legislation because it is always difficult, as in the case of weights and measures, to change old habits and old customs. The people of the province of Quebec are of a conservative disposition, generally speaking, and they are accustomed to see at the shy-e town the judge of the district. There they have the court of the district, the officers of the court, the residence of the judge, and all the social duties that the office of judge entails. Therefore it was in those days almost impossible to bring about the change which was the object of the legislation introduced by the then Attorney General of the province, the present Postmaster General. But quite a change has taken place in the province of Quebec, and I think that if my hon. friend would have a friendly round-table conference with the Attorney General, the Bar, and the judges of the province of Quebec, he could bring about the change that I am advocating. So that, after all, we can increase the number of the judges in the province of Quebec by bringing about that change, so as as to give justice to the litigants. I do not advocate at the present time any increase in the number of the judges, although by the change which would come as the result of the conference of my hon. friend with the Attorney General and judges of the province of Quebec, my hon. friend would not overburden his appropriation. In the province of Quebec we have now many judges of the Superior Court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are forty-five or
forty-six.

Anyway, there are not
more than fifty. If we compare the number of judges in Quebec with the number in Ontario, we will see that the difference is very great in favour of Ontario.
At six o'clock the House resumed and then took recess.
At eight o'clock the House resumed and again went into committee on Bill No. 68, relating to the Superior Courts of Saskatchewan and to amend the Judges Act; Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.

When the House took recess at six o'clock I was about to give a few facts and figures. By consulting Cartwright's Annual, .published in Toronto, I have ascertained the population of Quebec, Ontario and the_ Maritime Provinces, and also the number of judges in each province. According to the last census, the population of Quebec was 2,346,000; the population of Ontario was 2,725,000; and the population of the Maritime Provinces was 1,109,000. I find that for our population in Quebec, namely 2,346,000, we have 75 judges, 52 of these being Superior Court judges and 23 magistrates. I have found that in the province of Ontario, with a population of 2,725,000, they have 343 judges, 250 of these being magistrates and 93 High Court judges, and, I suppose, County Court judges. In the Maritime Provinces, with a population of 1,109,000, there are 112 judges, magistrates and County Court judges. I have not a detailed statement of the number of County Court judges and magistrates in the Maritime Provinces. It is not at all surprising, in view of the large population of the province of Quebec and the antiquated system of judicial districts in force there, that with the increase in the judicial business of large districts like Montreal, Quebec and Three Rivers, there should be many complaints on the part 'oi litigants. In order to show the disproportion between the number of judges and the business in the various districts, I shall give a few .statistics published by the Department of the Provincial Secretary in Qudbae. I find these in a blue-book, "Judicial Statistics for the year 1914." This book contains information concerning the Commissioner's Court, the Recorder's Court, the Justices of the Peace, the Court of the Sessions of the Peace, the District Magistrate's. Court, the Circuit Court, the Superior Court, the Court of Review, the Court of the King's Bench, the Sheriff's, and the Registrar's. Let us take the Recorder's Court. In cities and towns in the province of Quebec, for the year 1913-1914, which are the last available statistics, I find that the total number of complaints for the whole province was 33,518.

How many judges did
the hon. member say there were in the Maritime Provinces?
I said that of magistrates, judges and County Court judges, there were 112.	,

Magistrates	are noi
paid by the Federal Government, only the County and Superior Court judges.
I do not think it would be fair to count the magistrates and judges in together. The magistrates are as thick as blackberries, but there are only about 14 judges in Nova Scotia.

I know, but I am speaking of the total number of those who administer justice, both civil and criminal. It is for the sake of argument. I am not disputing that the magistrates are paid by the provinces; our magistrates are also. I find that in the year 1913-14 we had 33,518 cases in the Recorder's Court, of which 27,106 complaints were made in the city of Montreal alone. In order to show the disproportion in the administration of justice as between the different districts, if we take the other large districts, take Quebec for instance, we find that there were only 3,342 cases before that court. I now pass to the justices of the peace. I find that the number of complaints sensibly diminished on an average from the quinquennial period of 1905-09, to that of 1910-14, from 6,302 to 4,102. Still, in 1914 the number of complaints was larger by 171 than in the previous year. For the year 1913-14 there were in the whole province 2,264 cases before the justices of the peace, and of this total number Montreal alone gave 718 cases.
Let us take the comparative statements of the number of cases before the Courts of Sessions of Montreal and Quebec for the same period, 1913-14. It will be noticed here that there were 652 convictions in speedy trials in 1914 against 576 in 1913. To these figures Montreal alone contributed 638 in 1914 and 565 in 1913. Let us come now to the Circuit Court. The writs of summons for the average year of the three of 1910-14 numbered 4,407. But for the years 1910-14, on an average, Montreal alone contributed 23,832. The contested cases increased from 4,138 in 1913 to 6,238. Of course, out of the total number of summons issued many are disposed of without any contestation.
Now I pass from the Circuit Court to the Superior Court, and there I find again a very large disproportion. The number of

writs issued for any amount passed from 11,028 for the average year of the period 1905-09, to 15,653 on an average for the period 1910-15, or an increase of 4,635, equal to 42 per cent. The activity of the Superior Court was manifested in 1914 when 21,007 writs of summons issued as against 17,786 in 1913. Of this number Montreal contributed 2,800 additional while in Quebec the number was slightly higher. In the years 1913-1914, out of the total number of writs issued, namely, 21,070, Montreal alone contributed 12,886. I take the Court of Review. The number of cases inscribed in this court has more than doubled in ten years, but the increase has been most marked in the last quinquennial period from 1910 to 1914. The number of cases inscribed from 1905 to 1909 was 319 and from 1910 to 1914 it was 490. Take now the comparative statements of the Court of Review at Montreal and at Quebec during 1913-1914. The Montreal court rendered 390= judgments and the Quebec court 104. You can see the disproportion there again. The same disproportion exists in the Court of King's Bench. Whilst in Quebec 67 cases were heard during the years 1913 and 1914, 164 were heard in Montreal. I would suggest to my hon. friend the' Minister of Justice to initiate, at . the earliest possible moment, a conference between, let us say, representatives of the Bar, the Judiciary, the Attorney General of Quebec and himself, so that a reform might be brought about which will remedy the present unsatisfactory situation. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice is well aware that there are loud complaints not only from the ranks of the legal fraternity, not only from the judges themselves who would like to perform their duties in a speedy way, but from the business men from the boards of trade and from litigants, and it seems to me that the Minister of Justice, who is so conversant with the situation, in Montreal and in the province of Quebec generally, should see that a reform is brought about. The time has come for reform. A system which has been in existence since before Confederation was good enough when the demands upon the judiciary were much less than they are to-day. Various rural districts took some pride in their judges residing in the shire town and in the officers of the court remaining in the various districts. The officers of the court can remain there but in the interest of the administration of justice I think we should have the system, which prevails in Ontario-and other provinces. In Ontario, for in-

23&3
stance, they have the judges domiciled in Toronto. In tRe province of Quebec we will always have the old rivalry between Quebec and Montreal. But, let us see the judges domiciled at a central point, as in the province of Ontario, and then spreading themselves throughout the various districts and changing districts at every session- of the court. In that way there would be less prejudice against the judges, it would be more in harmony with the feelings of the judges themselves; justice would be more respected and the districts of Montreal and Quebec which are the largest, would have, the whole year round, the value of the presence of these judges to take up the cases which are coming before the courts. These judges would have the benefit of the experience of their brother judges and also the advantage of the law libraries of those cities. I do not say that my hon. friend should increase, with the present system, the number of judges, because I know the difficulties which always surround him. In certain districts like Gaspe, Rimouski, St. Johns, St. Hyacinthe and Richelieu, the judges will admit themselves that they are . not busy more than five or ten days during the month. If they were transferred to Montreal, from where they could travel to other districts the administration of justice would benefit. I have to apologize to the House for having brought this matter up on this Bill but I thought the ques tion germane to the principle involved.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I shall have very
much pleasure, indeed, if my hon. friend does not see fit to do it himself and save me the trouble, to transmit his speech to his friend, and my friend, Sir Lomer Gouin, the Attorney General of Quebec. It sounds very like what I have, in the course of quite a number of conversations, had occasion to point out to the attorney general of the province. There is not any doubt that there is loud complaint, and a very real grievance, in the district of Montreal, but that grievance exists, not because the province of Quebec has not a sufficient number of judges but because, being supplied with a sufficient number of judges, it is pleased to badly distribute them. The remedy is absolutely in the hands of the provincial authorities. I particularly desire to make that clear because I saw it recently reported-I do not know whether it was correctly reported or not- that the Attorney General of Quebec had said in the Legislature that he would provide for no further judges in the district of Montreal because the Minister of Justice . had said that the Dominion Government were not prepared to provide additional salaries for additional judges. It is quite true that I have said, following absolutely the line of argument of the hon. member for Rouville, that the evil lay in the had distribution of the number of judges and that I would not feel justified in increasing the number of judges provided for the province, to meet a difficulty resulting exclusively from the fact that the province, being provided- with a sufficient number of judges, chose to so badly distribute them that some of them have nothing to do while on the other hand, in the district of Montreal, there is very much more than work enough for the judges allocated to that district. Without waiting for the suggestion of the hon. member for Rouville, I have had occasion to discuss this subject with the Attorney General of the province. I may say that the acting chief justice of the province of Quebec has also made representations to me as to the necessity for a change in the system, very much, if not entirely, on the line suggested, 'by the hon. member for Rouville. I told him, as I have told everybody else who has spoken to me on the subject, that so far as I had any say in the matter I would be most happy to endorse any efforts to bring about an improvement of the system. But I can do no more than advise. I have no more to say about it than has the hon. member for Rouville, or any other gentleman who may be interested in the administration of justice in the province of Quebec. The matter is absolutely and, entirely in the hands of the provincial authorities, and I am sorry that they have not found it possible to bring about the obvious remedy-a redistribution of the judges-which it is within their power to make, and within their power exclusively. I do not understand that the hon. member for Rouville suggests that the province has not enough judges; we have not had that established. But what is established is that the province may distribute the judges as it sees- proper. I should be glad to see a reform in that direction, and so far as my advisory voice goes-, and so far as any endorsement coming from me would be useful, I shall be most happy to help. I have already had occasion to speak on this subject with the Attorney General and the acting chief justice of the province, and as a result of our discussion I understand that the acting

chief justice is bringing the matter before the provincial authorities, with the endorsement of the bar, and certainly with mine. If it were in my power to hasten in any way the remedying of the present state of affairs I should certainly 'be more than glad to do it. As the hon. member for Eouville has said, a great many years ago my hon*. friend the Postmaster General, then Attorney General of the province, introduced a measure seeking to bring about that reform. Unfortunately it did not meet with the support necessary to carry the proposal, and I am not aware that the effort has ever been renewed. I have been glad to hear what the hon. member for Eouville has said, because I trust that it will have weight in the quarters where the power is to remedy the evil complained of. In the meantime, I think it is only fair that it should be made quite clear to the people in the district of Montreal, who, as I have said, and as the hon. member for Eouville has demonstrated, have a very real grievance, that the cause of the grievance is not to be found here, but in the system which is maintained by the will of the legislature of the province of Quebec, and which can only Ire altered by that legislature, at the instance of those who have the leadership.

Is it not a fact that in
the province of Quebec there are not more than half a dozen judges living in the rural districts? The rest of them are living in the cities of Montreal, Quebec, Sherbrooke and Three Eivers. My experience is that as soon as a judge is' appointed he removes to one of the big cities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The provincial legislature determines where the judges shall reside. There are 41 Superior Court ,judges in the province of Quebec. Twenty are resident-I am speaking of their legal residences-in the city of Montreal, six in the city of Quebec, two in the city of Sherbrooke, and two in the city of Three Eivers. Then there are fifteen rural districts, in each of which there is one reisdent judge.
I think the minister would find it hard to find fifteen judges in the rural parts of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course, I do not follow the judges around to see whether they are obeying the law. I was speaking on the assumption that the judges reside .where the law says they ought to reside,

and I have no knowledge of disobedience to that law on the part of the judges. If there are jpdges who are not conforming to the law in that respect, I regret the fact; though I do not know that I can say more on the subject at the moment.

I do not claim that they are violating the law, but I do say that they must have received permission from some authority to reside in the cities, because with few exceptions all the judges	reside in	the cities.	For
instance, the judge for Gaspe lives in Quebec, the judge for St. Hyacinthe lives in Montreal, the judge for Pontiac lives in Westmount, and so on down the list. So they have plenty of judges in Montreal, but whether they are properly distributed or not I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There are twenty-one judges whose residences are legally fixed in the city of Montreal. That also is determined by the Provincial Legislature; so if the hon. member for Eouville thinks there are too few judges in Montreal, and the hon. member for Bonaventure thinks there are too many in Montreal and too few in the rural districts, I can only refer them both to the authority that .alone is competent to deal with the question. For myself, I share the view of the hon. member for Eouville that the workers should be *sent where the work is, and if that were done I think there would be less ground for complaint with regard to the sufficiency of the number of judges provided. The twenty or twenty-one judges in the district of Montreal are not, as the hon. member for Eouville has demonstrated, in proportion to the work that has to be done there. The problem, however, is one to .be solved by the Provincial authorities. I share the views of the hon. member for Eouville, and I shall be glad to do everything in. my power to bring about a system that will bring the work and the workers together, in preference to a system under which a large number of workers are scattered around where there is not enough work for one man to dp. I know that there still persists in the rural districts a desire to have a resident judge, whether the work to be done justifies it or not, and I realize that that makes a difficulty in the way of those who seek to bring about the reform which the hon. member for Eouville advocates, and which has my sympathy.	.

I am very pleased to learn that the distribution of judges is vested in the provincial- authorities, and that the Minister of Justice is in no way responsible. I wish to draw his attention here, and in this way to a matter about which I have already spoken to him, and that is the very small remuneration of the County Court judges in the city of Vancouver. Compared with judges in other parts, they have a very wide jurisdiction. The County Court judge in our city has a jurisdiction in debt and damage up to $1,000, and a jurisdiction in equity up to' $2,500. This, I think, is very much in advance of the jurisdiction of County Court judges in any other province and yet these judges receive a salary of ,only $3,000 a year, which is entirely inadequate. The barristers of Vancouver and, I think, of British Columbia met some time ago and passed a very strong resolution on this subject, feeling that the judges of the county courts are underpaid, and their work, I know, is of a very heavy character. A year ago, when the fall session opened, there were over three hundred cases on the list awaiting the judges, an -almost insuperable task for them, and I simply take this opportunity of calling the matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice. I understand that it is rather difficult for him to deal with the matter now, but I do wish that he would take it into consideration and deal with it as early as it is possible for him to reach that phase of the subject.
Mr. .ROGERS: I am going to try to bring the House hack to order again. We have been discussing the judges in the various provinces of the Dominion of Canada. I would like to say a word about the judges mentioned in the Bill before the committee.
Mr-. LEMIEUX: Carried. Why do you obstruct the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
My hon. friend has been obstructing it for several hours. Surely I am entitled to say a word in regard to the matter. I see by the Bill that:
The salaries of the judges of the Court of Appeal and of His Majesty's Court of King's Bench for Saskatchewan shall he as follows:
The Chief Justice of Saskatchewan If he is also the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal, and if not, to the Chief Justice of Appeal.
Then again there comes the Chief Justice of the Court of King's Bench; does my hon.
friend propose to have three chief justices within the province of Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The same question was asked this afternoon by the right hon. leader of the Opposition. It is . not intended to have more than two chief justices, but the provision that is placed in the Bill with, regard to the Chief Justice of Saskatchewan, as -my hon. colleague will notice, is restricted by the condition:
-if he is also the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal, and if not, to the Chief Justice of Appeal.
There is at present a chief justice of Saskatchewan, who is the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. There is only one high court there. The gentleman who holds that title may or may not be appointed Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal or Chief Jus- ' tioe of the Court of King's Bench. What is desired to make clear is that the mere title of Chief Justice of Saskatchewan does not carry with it the right to the salary of $8,000. It is the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal who is to have the $8,000 salary; if he happens to be the Chief Justice of Saskatchewan, why, he will have that salary just the same. If the Chief Justice of Saskatchewan does not happen to be appointed Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal he will simply retain the salary pertaining to the position which he at present holds. We do not intend to make any special salary because of the holding of the title of Chief Justice of Saskatchewan.

Is that not unusual? In all the other provinces the Chief Justice of the province is President of the Court of Appeal. This is the first instance in- which the Chief Justice of a province may not be the President, of the Court of Appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the province of Quebec, for example, there is not any chief justice who is designated by the title of the Chief Justice of Quebec. We have the Chief Justice of the King's Bench and the Chief Justice of the Superior Court, both of them in the province of Quebec, and, by courtesy I have no doubt, the people designate the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal as the Chief Justice of Quebec, but he is not officially designated as the Chief Justice of Quebec. In the province of Saskatchewan there is to be a Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal and a Chief Justice of the Court of King's	Bench;-I
think that is the court of first instance that is provided for. Perhaps

it was not necessary to mention in the Bill the Chief Justice of Saskatchewan, but the draftsman mentioned it because it happened that the Chief Justice of the only court that is there is designated as the Chief Justice of Saskatchewan, and this provision is inserted in order to make it clear that the salary is assigned to the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal. If the Chief Justice of Saskatchewan is appointed Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal, of course, he will have the salary attached to that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: As I understand from my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, although the present Chief Justice of Saskatchewan is named in this Bill, it does not necessarily follow that he will be the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly not.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: He might be the Chief Justice of the Court of King's Bench.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

In the province of Ontario there is the Supreme Court of Ontario composed of two divisions, the Appellate Division and the High Court Division, but the Chief Justice of the province is the president of the Appellate Division.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. PROllLX:	It has always been the
case in Ontario that the Chief Justice of the province is the Chief Justice of the Court of Appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand that in Ontario there has been a Chief Justice designated as the Chief Justice of Ontario, and I believe that is also the case in Saskatchewan; but, as I pointed out, it is not so in all the provinces.

I see that in this year
of war there is an increase here of $14,000 for investigations of ore deposits, economic minerals, etc. Would not the hon. minister think it wiser to go slowly on these new things when we need the money so badly for war purposes, when our debt is increasing so rapidly, when we have just made provision for another war loan of $75,000,000, with another one to come in a very short time? Does it not strike him that some of these things that would be necessary and useful for the development in Canada in time of peace might well be delayed a little under present conditions? How can he explain satisfactorily this increase of $14,000 at this time when the country is looking to us to economize in everything that is not absolutely necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I think this item reflects credit on the department. The same item in 1915-16 was $86,000, and so this is a decrease in the vote for the coming year. I should say it was a noble effort to economize.
It does not say so in the Estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, this vote was reduced in the Estimates from $86,000 to $62,000. The latter sum proved insufficient to carry on efficiently the work of the branch. In addition, a new division, that of ceramics, has been organized during the year.
Will the minister please explain that;, has it to do with the ancient Assyrian potteries?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada

speechtext: I understand that it is quite commendable that the department should experiment with a view to the future, in order to manufacture in our own country goods that we have hitherto imported possibly some from countries that we will not want to import from after the war is over. But I woulld like more particulars from the minister as to this one particular item. He tells us this is a reduction. It is an increase, according to the Estimates. The vote last year was $62,000 and this year it is $76,000, and the minister tells us this is not sufficient for the work done in 1915-16. How did he get the money to make the expenditure, $85,000?

While the minister is answering, he might also explain to the committee how it comes that the minister who preceded him spent as travelling expenses for the Mines Branch $1,020.34, while the real head of the department, Dr. Haanel, spent only $118.10. The other scientists attached to the department have spent only small amounts aJlso. I find that Mr. Boyd spent $108, Mr. Brock $631, Mr. Bruce $50, Mr. Burling $67, and so on.
Coming to the merits of the case, I quite agree with the minister that this is a very important branch of the service. At the same time it is more or less experimental, and we cannot expect results in the immediate future, or even in the rather distant future. Having sat .in this House for the last twenty years, I know as a matter of fact that we have been testing peat bogs in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and other provinces as well, for about that length of time, and with no result. So, in these hard times, when the people are being bled white, when we are borrowing money from the Americans, when we are spending right and left for war purposes and other purposes, I think we can well afford to bring this estimate to the original figure and even wipe it out completely.
This is an item which could well come under the head of a technical institute or institute of technology, if we had one in Ottawa, and it was promised by some of my hon. friend's colleagues in the Government that we should have one. When I brought to the attention of the House the other day the question of technical education, I reminded the Minister of Labour that in 1909, when the question of technical education was brought up in the House on the motion of the member for South Wellington, tlhe Minister of Militia stated that we had in his country natural resources which were in the experimental stage, and which required the testing of our scientists. He said that the Government would be justified in having in Ottawa, for the benefit of industries growing out of these natural resources, an institute of technology. We go on testing every year on ceramics, peat bogs,, ore dressing and metallurgical processes, but with no avail; whereas if we had an institute of technology from>
which all the provinces would derive some benefit, it might be of general advantage to the country to spend the money that we are spending in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The increase of $14,000 is accounted for as follows: Ceramic division, $6,000. I have just given the committee the details of that amount. $6,000 are required for additional equipment to the ore-dressing laboratory. The class of work now coming to the laboratory requires that a free screening ball mill of the Gates type, and a Wilfley table, be installed. The installation of a small electric furnace, and necessary equipment is contemplated. For field expenses, including collection of samples, investigations, and all travelling expenses, including contingencies in connection with the work of the division, $2,440 is required.

The Minister of
Finance always gives us a great homily about his financing. Last year it was patriotism and production; this year it is to be economy all along the line-Allison and commissions, an hon. member suggests. He and his colleagues, when they get through with these homilies, one after the other tell us: We cannot save anything; we cannot make this item less than it was last year; there is this to be done and there is that to be done. All this would be very beautiful and very lovely if the people of this country were not being compelled to submit to direct taxation for the first time. Allison can get off with a swag of three-quarters of a million, and no investigation, hut hon. gentlemen in the Government, with the responsibility of ministers, ask this Parliament and this country _to give them just as much money as they require, as if no war was going on and as if conditions were normal. This minister is in the same position as all the
9 p.m. rest. Has it dawned on my hon.
friend that when he comes to Parliament with an estimate of this kind, he is coming under exceptional conditions? Does he realise that a war is going on, that there must be economy, that the people are being subjected to direct taxation for the first time? This work in connection with ceramics, and the other things to which my hon. friend refers, might be all right in normal times, but the explanation that my hon. friend has made with regard to the necessity for this expenditure is of no value in this year of grace 1916, having regard to the present conditions. The explanation that the hon. minister has given us is made without regard to the fact that there is war, or to the fact that there is taxation. Will the minister be good enough to tell us whether he took into consideration the

necessity for economy when he drafted this estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This branch is a branch for publication and investigation. I think it is more important than ever, even in this time of war, that every possible effort should be made to obtain information as to the natural resources of the country. I have no other answer to give the hon. gentleman.
Does my hon. friend not think that he should economize in his department, in view of the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: 1 have stated that the expenditure of this branch in 1914 was $85,000. This amount was afterwards reduced to $62,000, which has been found insufficient. In order to help the country, and to fulfil the duties that are imposed upon this branch, we require an additional amount of $14,000 for the purpose which 1 have stated.

Will the minister tell me if any people who go into the mining business ever use his reports? I get them constantly, and frequently send them out to mining men, but they do not pay any attention to them so far as I know. They always investigate for themselves; they do not rely at all on my hon. friend's reports. If that is the case why go to this expense?" Last year the minister's predecessor told us a long and beautiful story about how they were making peat down here in Alfred. You know that they are not making any peat for commercial purposes, although the Government have spent money year after year. I told the minister at that time that mo benefit would accrue to the country from these peat tests, and that they were on the wrong track. Apparently they were. The minister told us then that private parties had taken over the peat deposits and were making peat commercially for the people. Aly hon. friend knows that is not correct, and that the production of peat has not been a commercial success.

My hon. friend from Oxford (Air. Nesbitt) is mistaken in respect to the peat industry, especially with regard to the manufacture of peat in my county. Some thousands of tons have been manufactured since 1912. Last summer they manufactured 9,000 tons, some of which is now on sale in Ottawa by Mr. Donnelly. There is now some 600 tons on sale at Alfred, by Mr Daoust and Air. Belanger who exploited the

plant last summer under rental from the Canada Peat Society, with which Mr. Moore and Mr. Shuttleworth are associated. Peal is a good substitute for coal, and I would urge the department to encourage the industry as much as possible. I would especially urge on the Minister of Public Works that he should heat the public buildings of Canada with peat, with a view tc advertising it as a substitute for coal and furnishing a good example. Experiments have shown that it is a good substitute for coal, especially for grates. A report has recently been published showing large areas of peat lands in different parts of Canada. Coal for the use of the central provinces must be imported from Pennsylvania and in case of a shortage of coal or of unusually high prices, such as we experienced a few years ago, peat forms a valuable substitute. The plant at Alfred is complicated, and all the machinery has been imported from Sweden. The Government bought ,300 acres there, and have exploited not more than 10 acres.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The remarks of my hon. friend, I think, justify the department from the standpoint both of experimentation and of publication. In 1910 the Government of the day decided to buy a certain peat bog in Alfred, Ont., in order to make experiments. The cost of the purchase of the peat bog and the installation of the original plant was as follows:	Purchase of bog,
$1,874.84; building two peat sheds, blacksmith shops, office, platform for loading peat into cars, and movable house for peat machinery, $1,844; rail-way sidings, $500; machinery brought from Sweden, $7,600; blacksmith tools and implements, $863.78; labour preparing bog, draining, levelling, including salary of manager, $3,722; sundries, travelling expenses, $380; total, $17,122.15. This was for 'the purchase and installation of the plant. The labour cost of operating peat manufacturing plant during the two seasons 1910 and 1911 was for 1910, $2,857.08, and for 1911, $3,107.54, making a total of $6,764.62, which includes the salary of the manager for those seasons. To this figure must be added for new implements bought $183, repairs, etc., $427.24, living expenses $46, quilts and blankets $158, loading peat $282.30, which makes a total for the season, of 1911 of $5,022.15. The cost of operating for the two seasons 1910 and 1911 is therefore $7,879.23. This brings the total expenditure on bog, including capital expenditure, to $26,023.73, which includes freight
and cartage on the peat sold towards the latter part of 1911. The bog, exclusive of machinery, tools, stock, etc., but including railway sidings, was sold to private parties for the sum of $2,284.25.

Does that include the
peat?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes. Mr. G. M. Shuttleworth was the party who purchased it. and he sold it afterwards to the Canadian Peat Society.

Did you go out of the
business?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The Government ceased exploiting the bog for reasons which I shall give later on, and preferred to allow outside parties to find out by experience the best means of producing peat.
The Government became discouraged.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No.
They have great courage if they did not.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Personally, I am sorry that this Government property has been sold. I have had no time to go into all the details, which might have resulted in a revision of my opinion, but I feel very sorry that the bog was transferred to outside parties. I want to give these details to the House because they have been asked for .on a number of occasions in the past.
Not to interrupt the hon.-gentleman I can tell him where he can get other bogs if he is sorry about selling this.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:

speechtext: Yes, they are using peat every day at the concentration plant in Ottawa. Experience has shovfn that it is the best and cheapest gas producer. In fairness to the industry, .1 think I should read a few sentences I picked from a report. This will give my hon. friends an idea of the utility of the department's publications.

I do not think we are very much interested in hearing that; we pan read the reports ourselves. We are asked to vote $63,000 in this item. The minister has given a long explanation, but it referred entirely to the peat that had been sold; he has not told us what is going to be done with this $63,000. How much of it will be spent in peat investigation, and what is the minister's policy in this respect?

The minister was answering a question I asked, and he has answered it conclusively, to my mind. He said that we have spent $18,000 in experiments on peat, and that it has not been a commercial success. I know other people who have experimented with peat, and have not made a commercial success of it. With all due deference to my hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx), those friends of his who turned out nine hundred tons of peat last summer would have to turn that much out in a week, if it was to compete at $3 a ton with anthracite coal at $7 a ton. If my hon. friend invests any money with those friends of his he will be sorry only once,

and that will be all the time. My hon. friend read something about a weatherdrying process for peat, and said that somebody 'had told him that that was the usual process in Russia. Now, to my certain knowledge, it is not the process used ip Russia, for they use very strong hydraulic pressure, and make a peat that is something worth while. We are still continuing experiments in Canada with the dry air process. It has never been a commercial success-, and I doubt if it ever wil-l be, because, as the drying process continues, the briekettes disintegrate.' That is why that process will never be a commercial success. My hon. friend from Prescott ought to have turned out the 900 tons he speaks of for $18,000, and I guarantee it cost three times that. My hon. friend knows that Shuttleworth did not make a success of it either. W'hat I object to is thiat the department should continue investigating ore deposits, economic minerals, peat deposits, etc., when the public has never received any benefit from their reports in the past. I do not think there is a mining man in Canada who uses the department's reports on these deposits. If a man has any sense he will find out for himself before he invests his money, and if he has not any sense he will 1-ose his money anyway.

I find in the Auditor General's report, 1914-15, that the expenditure of the Department of Mines for that year was $759,862.46. The Estimates this year are $937,000, a difference of $178,000, roughly speaking. Now, the complaint I have is that ministers ask us to vote money without ever having sat down and considered their Estimates with relation to present war-time conditions. Let us see how some of the moneys of the Canadian people were spent last year. Under the Geological Survey Branch, I find that a gentleman by the name of J.'D. Evans, of Trenton, disposed of a collection of insects to the Government for $2,000. Now, what in the name of all that is decent and sensible, does this country want to buy $2,000 worth of insects for in war time? The Foote Mineral Company, of Philadelphia-no truck or trade with the Yankees -got $3,874.96 for meteorites, agate, sero-lites, and siderites, and uraninites. Then a gentleman by the name of S. G. Ford, of St. John's, Newfoundland, disposed of an Eskimo bird-skin suit to an unsuspecting Government, who alleged that they were trying to economize, for $35. S. H. Harris,
of London, England, had a collection of Indian and Esquimaux native articles, which he sold to the Government for $500. E. W. Hawkes, of Ottawa, sold some Eskimo specimens, models, one limestone kettle, one walrus tusk, and sundry other specimens to the Government for $675, in war time. Then there was a lady called Mrs. O. Heidemann-it sounds German- who lived in Forest Glenn, Md., and who got $210 for some enlarged models of insects. Then the Government went down to Old Town, Maine, and bought a collection of Micmao Indian relics from G. A. Paul)-I do not know whether he was an Indian-for $175. Mr. A. B. Regan, Nett Lake, Minnesota, received $50 for Medicine lodge parchment; manuscript, 20 pages, $20; birch bark phonograph records, $50.50. There is a messenger pigeon, $50, and then in Philadelphia some gentleman by the name of Shotridge sold a Chilkat blanket for $200. Mr. F. G. Speck of Philadelphia sold Labrador, Eskimo, Montagnais and Micmac specimens for $38; Micmac-Montagnais collection from Newfoundland, $153; Abenaki, Penobscot, Temagami specimens, $53; Iroquois specimens, $69; drafting map, $12; a total of $325; and so on right through the list, collections of birds, etc. No less a sum of money than $607.10 was spent on freight to the express companies. These absurd and ridiculous purchases in war time meant a total expenditure of $15,585 for which this minister in previous year took the money of the people of Canada, which they were taxed directly to obtain. What I say to my hon. friend-and I do not say it to him more than to any of the other members-is that no minister has yet come before this committee this session who has shown the slightest appreciation of the fact that in this year we must economize as we have never economized before. The war has made no difference to them. The taxation has made no difference. My hon. friend is going on purchasing these geological curiosities just the same as if everything was all right, although all this money is being dug out of the pockets of the people of this country. Does my hon. friend mean to say that he would defend such absurd expenditure during this year? Is he going to spend a dollar along those lines? Cannot >
the people of Canada wait for these Eskimo specimens and relics and other peculiarities to be gathered until we have plenty of money in the treasury? $15,000 is $15,000 at the present time. Some company in this

country that has been struggling along without a dividend until the 1st of January, 1915, will be compelled to disgorge a portion of that $15,000, and my hon. friend will take it, not for the war, but for buying birds' nests and Miemac relics. Is my hon. friend going to do that this year? Why does he not reduce the Estimate by the amount of money that he spent last year on such things?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
As I have already stated, we have been doing our best to decrease all the expenditures of this department, but at the same time I may safely state that the needs of this department are increasing every day, and I think if we stand by the expenditure of last year we shall be doing extremely well. We have cut a good many expenditures that we deemed very expedient to make this year; we have cut - out an old appropriation for the building of an experimental station for explosives, in order to put into force the Explosives Act which was passed by this House. We have not spent and we do not intend to spend a cent on that in order to save money in this time of war. We are, however, asking this House to vote what we deem to be absolutely necessary to carry out the objects of this branch. If my hon. friends are anxious to have the details of this vote,
I can give them. These are the details of the expenditure in the branch of the Metalliferous Division, $2,500. Molybdenum and copper. The bulletins issued by this department are asked for and we cannot sup- , ply the demand in this country and in all European countries. Throughout the whole world in fact, these bulletins are in great demand. The first edition of our bulletin on molybdenum has been exhausted and the demand is such that a new edition is required as soon as possible. This will be prepared by Dr. Wilson and much new material on the metallurgy of molybdenum will be incorporated in this reprot.
Dr. Wilson has been preparing a series of reports on the copper resources of Can-. ada and the associated industries. The third report of the series on copper and copper mining in Canada is in course of preparation.
In regard to this item I might ask my hon. friends if they do not think that it is most important that experiments should be proceeded with on molybdenum and copper, and that these bulletins are of great interest, not only to Canada, but to people in other countries where there is capital

that may be invested in the development of these mines.
There is $6,000 for the continuation of the investigations into the iron ore resources of Canada. Two field parties are proposed, and areas in Canada not yet examined by the engineers engaged on this work will be surveyed during the field season. The location of the parties cannot be determined until the close of the present field season, but one party will probably be sent to British Columbia. I would draw the attention of iny hon. friends to this item and ask them if they do not think it is to the interest of Canada that we should proceed with this work.
Mining and metallurgical industries of Canada, $1,500. Under the general direction of Mr. John McLeish, chief of the division of Mineral Resources and Statistics, a new edition of our report on the Mining and Metallurgical Industries of Canada is in course of preparation. The first volume dealing with the metal mines and smelters is to be prepared by Mr. Bolton, in association with Dr. Wilson, chief engineer of the Metal Mines Division. This report will -contain a brief business statement of the organization and equipment of the various operating companies in Canada and is of the nature of a business directory.
There is $2,000 for the Non-metalliferous Division, limestones and their uses. Limestones of special grade are required in large quantities for the manufacture of calcium carbide, wood pulp and paper, glassware, limes, cements, plasters and for numerous other purposes. The department is endeavouring to obtain full information regarding the limestone resources of the various provinces and their suitability for various uses. During the field seasons of 1914 and 1915, Mr. Frechette has been examining the limestones of the province of Quebec and collecting samples. The laboratory investigation of these samples is now in progress. It is proposed that this work be extended to the province of Ontario during the season of 1916 as the results are of immediate importance to many industries and particularly to the manufactures of wood pulp and paper.
There is an item of $1,000 for the investigation of certain non-metallic minerals. Mr. de Schmid has been preparing a series of special monographs regarding one occurrence in Canada, the mining, and preparation for the market of certain non-metallic minerals, including mica, apatite, and feldspar. Reports relating to these materials have already been published or will be

issued shortly. Other materials for which we have received inquiries are to be investigated as far as possible. They include barytes, pyrolusite, talc, fluor-spar and infusiorial earth. There is a constant demand for these minerals from Canadian manufacturing industries, and also from the United States. Previous to the present war, supplies were drawn from foreign countries, but these have been cut off. It is, therefore, important that this work should be continued as expeditiously as possible. The next item is for $2,500. Sands and their Uses. While there are in Canada very extensive deposits of loose sands, sandstones and similar materials, no systematic study has been made of them from an economic point of view. The sands are put to a multitude of uses, and many different grades of material, varying in character, position' and physical properties, are required for industrial purposes. Supplies formerly imported from Europe for the manufacture of glassware are now cut off. Some sands used in the ceramic industry were also imported from Europe and in part from the United States. Moulding sand is largely imported from the United States. In building construction, immense quantities of sand are employed, often without sufficient attention to the nature and quality of the material and its suitability for the work required. The strength and durability of imortars and cements depend in part upon the kind of sand used. It was, therefore, deemed advisable to institute technical investigations of sands and related materials which occur in Canada; to ascertain if we do not possess materials in every way equal to the imported sands used in the various industries, and to study sand deposits in the vicinity of the principal industrial centres to ascertain their nature and their value for industrial purposes. In addition to the field work in sand deposits, this investigation will include a series of physical tests at the departmental laboratories, as well as in a commercial foundry to ascertain their, qualities under actual working conditions. Mr. Cole has been investigating sand deposits in Quebec for two seasons, and has extended his investigation into Ontario. It is proposed that this work shall be continued in Ontario in 1916. There is an item of $4,000 for the continuation of the examination of the bituminous sands of Alberta. Also, there is $3,500 for the examination of the building stones of Canada. During the past five field seasons
Dr. W. A. Parks, of the Royal Ontario Museum, has been engaged in the work of preparing a series of monographs on the building and ornamental stones of Canada. Volumes dealing with Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime Provinces have been published. The fourth volume on the Central Western Provinces is in course of preparation. It is proposed that the work in 1916 be carried on in the province of British Columbia preparatory to the report on the building stones in that province, which will complete the series.
I pass now to the Fuels and Fuel-testing Division. This vote is for the salaries of the employees, additional labour which may be required from time to time in connection with the investigations conducted in our laboratories, technical assistants, chemists, and technical engineers who may be required for temporary work in connection with the investigations carried on in the fuel-testing laboratories and field work. According to arrangements made some time ago this branch is conducting large-scale tests on commercial samples of coal obtained from operating mines of Eastern and Western collieries. The sample of coal, approximately thirty tons in weight, is furnished free by the mine sampled, but the freight is paid by the department, special rates being granted by the railroads for this purpose. This money is for the purpose of defraying the cost of carrying the coal from the mines to the experimental plant at Ottawa. The work includes the investigation of methods employed in Canada for the production of power, with a view to ascertaining the most efficient fuel to employ in the various sections interested. Money for this purpose was voted for 'two consecutive years, but the limited staff of the division made it impossible to use the money voted.
_Mr. GRAHAM: I do not wish to interfere with the minister, but I was going W suggest that this item .pass.
Carried.

No, not carried. I am glad to see the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) here and I hope he is taking in the essay which was being read by the Secretary of State. One thing we would like to know is the capacity and efficiency of the men who are in charge of these investigations. I suppose, to be fair to the minister, that he has to deal with what has been handed down to him in connection

with this department. I take it that all the operations of this department, under ordinary conditions, are useful and necessary. But we are more or less in the dark as to the men who are in charge of this work. We .are paying out money and we should like to know that we are paying it to the right class of men. We are curious to know who they are, where they received their education, .and what experience they have had in other places to enable them to obtain this information and perform these experiments. If they are only experimenting among themselves, or upon one another, with no particular knowledge about the business except yvhat they gather among themselves, I think the money is wasted. This is along the line of technical education, and that is why I am so glad that the Minister of Labour is here, so that he may see the necessity of' having first-class men connected with a piatter of this kind. I do not say we should not publish these reports. I think they are useful. But I think the minister should inquire how many of them he should issue. The demand, so far as Canada is concerned, must be somewhat limited. I .would like to see some reciprocity established between this department and the mining departments of the various provinces. I am not aware that there is very piuch exchange of knowledge between the .Department of Mines at Ottawa and the different mining offices and mining departments in the provinces. If information of that kind acquired among these mining engineers is of a reliable character, this money is well spent. But, if the engineers connected with the department are men who, .though they talk of mining coal and the working of a coal mine, and yet we have Reason to fear that if they were up against a coaJhmine there would be an explosion in a short time, that would be a different matter. I would suggest that we should have practical men connected with these things, and should establish institutions in Ottawa that would give technical education. If the minister will not do it in the different provinces, let us have one big institution in Ottawa in connection with this branch, in which our young men who desire to do so may qualify as engineers in the different branches spoken of by the minister.
At the head of this department let us have the very best men that the world can produce-or, to use the words of the Prime Minister, that science can devise or money buy. If this money is used along the line

of proper development, we do not begrudge it, but if it is wasted in useless experiments; if the work is not developed and expanded, I think we should begrudge the expenditure of this money. I heard the minister talk about the testing of coal. The coal mines in Canada are much older than Confederation, and I am surprised that it is only -lately that the department has acquired knowledge of the qualities of the different kinds of coal found in Canada. The minister mentioned the fact that thirty tons of coal were lately obtained from somewhere for testing purposes. If that is coal -that was never tested before, that is all right, but if up to this time we have not been able to obtain from his department a knowledge of the different qualities of the coal in Canada, I think we have been moving too slowly. I hope, in spending this $76,000 in these days of storm and stress for the education of the people along the lines suggested by the minister, that we are getting education that is first-class, not education that we shall have to unlearn when practical problems arise.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
In order to relieve the
mind of the hon. member, I refer him to the statute creating this department. By article 10 of the Geology and Mines Act, it is provided that:
No person shall he appointed to the department as an officer having- such special, professional or technical qualifications under schedule A of the Civil Service Act, unless he is a science graduate of either a Canadian or a foreign university, or of the Mining School of London or the Ecole des Mines of Paris, or of some recognized science school of standing equal to that of the said universities and schools, or a gradute of the Royal Military College.
We are doing our best to get the best men we can, but it is not very easy to get men who have bothi scientific knowledge and experience. I agree with my hon. friend that if technical schools could be developed in this country they would help us a great deal. The hon. gentleman has inquired about the testing of coal. We have' a plant for testing the calorific power of coal, peat, lignite, or any other fuel, in order to find out whether they can better be used as fuel or for the production of gas. The hon. gentleman suggests that the work of the department is not proceeding very fast. This department is, comparatively speaking, a new department; it was created only in 1907, and is far from being completely organized. In asking to-night for these amounts I am sure that I am not

asking for all the things that are necessary for the good operation of this department in the service of the country.

I do not want the committee to run away with the idea that the Mines Department is no good. My experience is quite different. I think we have some very good men in the Mines Department, who are doing very good work, and . I should like, if I say anything at all, to say a worc( to encourage the department. I think that it is creditable to the minister that he is making investigations and trying to disseminate knowledge among the people of Canada. As the Minister of Labour has gone to sleep during the last three or four years, and has utterly failed to do anything in the matter of technical education, it is to be commended that this minister has at least attempted to do something. In my province the Geological Survey has been of great advantage to the gold mining industry. By referring to the
10 p.m. plans that they have in the offices here a great deal of useful information can be obtained with regard to our gold mines in Nova Scotia. Every Nova Scotian who knows anything about the mining industry in that province will tell you that this work has been very useful. I had hoped that the minister would outline what he intends to do during the coming year, and tell us something, without reading from books, with regard to the work in his department. If he would promise that he will not spend the money that he is asking us to vote in the purchase of Indian blankets and relics of that kind, and that the money will be devoted to proper purposes and to maintain the good work done by the Mines Department, I should hold up both hands for having the item put through. He has not given us any explanation as to who is responsible for the expenditure of $15,000 for foolish relics last year. '	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It is a rather technical matter for me to give general statements without following my notes. I have tried my best to give some of the information coming from my department, and to impress on the members of the committee the purposes of the proposed expenditures. Of course, we will do our best to economize, but I must tell my hon. friend that in order to economize we shall have to fight against the interests of those who will benefit by this work. If the hon. gentleman wants us to proceed to make investigations,
and to buy the necessary things for the making of experiments in order to help the development of manufactures in this country, these appropriations are necessary.
Have any investigations been made with regard to the use of feldspar in the production of potash?

speechtext:
We are no longer experimenting with peat except by locating bogs, determining their area, and depth, and

testing samples in Ottawa to determine their calorific value and their gas producing power. That varies in different parts of the country.
Are other peat bogs being exploited?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I think there is one at
Farnham. My hon. friend will find literature on this subject in the Department of Mines that will interest him.

I have received some of that literature and it is very good. The difficulty with the peat industry is the lack of markets. Montreal coal merchants tell me that they have tried it as a substitute for coal and find it good, especially for grates, but there is not much demand for it, as the people find it takes more storage space than coal and the transportation charges are also quite heavy.

speechtext:
It is only in parts of
the country where wood and coal are dear that peat production has a chance to become a success. The general conclusion of all experimenters is that peat will be of general use in this country when coal reaches a price not much higher than it has to-day.
