article of general consumption for domestic purposes would we have an ample supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Reports are that we have immense areas of peat bogs all through the Dominion.

I should like to get the details of the travelling expenses of the former Minister of Mines. I find that as Minister of Mines he received $1,020.34 in 1915, and the same gentleman happened to be Secretary of State and he received in that capacity as travelling expenses, $600. That is to say, he received $1,620.34 as Minister of Mines and as Secretary of State. Why the distinction? When he was travelling as Minister of Mines did he deprive himself of his capacity as Secretary of State, and when he was Secretary of State did he travel without his dual personality as Minister of Mines? I say that this is simply scandalous and should not be allowed to pass.
Are the reports to which the minister referred a moment ago translated and would the minister be ready to give to the committee a list of the translators? I am informed that nearly all of the translation is made outside of the staff appointed a few years ago. I remember that my hon. friend

and a few others obtained the appointment of a staff of translators for the blue-books. I am informed that there are outside the Civil" Service, a large number of gentlemen who do translation, whereas a few years ago when the translators were appointed, it was perfectly understood that no more translation would be sent outside. I am bound to say that many of the reports which have been translated outside the department are translated very badly indeed, and do no credit to the translators who have been selected.
I am not speaking of the permanent officials; generally speaking they are very good officials, but there is some work being done outside of the official staff which is not creditable at all. I would like to know if my hon. friend has a list of the translators who receive work outside of the official staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: A distinction should be made between the staff of translators which was created a few years ago and the present translators of the Mines Branch. My hon. friend knows that the staff of -translators created two years ago was created to attend to the translation of blue-books and the documents passing through the House of Commons.

When the amount was voted in the House, and when that staff was created, my hon. friend said: Now, we shall never have to wait any more for blue-books; we are appointing a new staff, and the papers in the province of Quebec blazoned forth the patriotism of the hon. gentleman. He had obtained a large amount for the creation of that staff of French translators, and it was distinctly understood that no more work would be sent outside of the staff; whereas, at the present time, a large number of people are getting work from various departments, and especially- from his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
If my hon. friend understood the question of translation better he would not speak as he does. He knows that under the late Government money was expended for translation outside of the staff, and that bad translation was the result. There is now in each department a special translator. The Public Works Department, for instance, is entitled to a translator, and every year Parliament votes his salary. The same is true of the other departments. This work is altogether different from the general work of translation that is done for the House of Commons, and which consists of the translation of the reports of the dif-

ferent departments and all the literature that goes through the House. We have, for the House of Commons, two staffs of translators-the hlue-book staff and the Hansard staff. Their work is altogether different from that of which we are now speaking.
What are the names of the gentlemen who do translation work outside of the official staff of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I will give them in a minute. The Department of Mines and the Geological Survey are departments whose business is that of publications. The special work of these departments would be of no use if the results of their investigations and experiments were not published throughout the country. I think that the item for publication in my department amounts to $76,000 a year. It is the most important work of my department. Then, these are departments that require technical translators. Mr. Desaul-niers will tell you that when my department sends a report to him to be translated by his staff, he will not take the responsibility of asking his men, who are trained for the translation of blue-books, to undertake that special translation. We receive letters from almost every country in the world asking for these reports, all in Erench, these letters coming from Russia, Italy, the Balkans and even from Constantinople.
Who were the translators?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We take such translators as we can find. I admit that sometimes the translation is not as satisfactory as I would like. The gentleman who has charge of the work for the Mines Branch is Marc Sauvalle.

But he is the permanent official; he was appointed years ago. I am asking my hon. friend who are the gentlemen outside of the official staff who are doing this special work in the Mines Branch and the Geological Survey.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There are none. My hon. friend is aware that Mr. Marc Sauvalle is the gentleman who is in charge of this translation, hut he cannot do it alone. He does what he can but he has to ask for help. He is himself responsible for the engagment of these people. He is left free to take the translator tlhat he recommends to me.
Whom has he taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. J. E. Belanger.
Mr. LEMIiEUX: Where is he from?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot tell the hon. gentleman tout I will get all this information. Mr. C. R. Daoust, J. A. David, Theo. Denis, E. Dulieux, P. Edgerley, J. A. Fortier, Oscar Lanctot, J. H. O. Lang-lois, A. Mailhiot, J. H. Palardy, E. Roehon are for the Geological Survey Branch. For the Mines Branch the officials are:	A.
Bouesnel, J. L. Binet, O.M.I., B. H. Charle-bois, C. R. Daoust, D. Laframtooise, M. LeFranc, W. E. Morgan, A. A. Taillon.
Have you a man named Sauve?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have no man named Sauve, but I will bring a full list to-morrow and, give all the details.
Is Mr. David from Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know.- I might almost say that I do not know one of these people. I do not know that one of these men has 'been changed since I have been in this office.

I am not saying that my hon. friend bias been appointing them. Outside of Mr. Sauvalle, who has belonged to the official staff for many years, and who is a competent officer, and outside of two or three names which the minister gave to the House, I dare say there is not one competent translator for this technical work.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I will be most grateful to my hon. friend if he can recommend some competent man to me, and I will be very glad to take him.
It would be very easy for my hon. friend if, instead of appointing translators for political purposes, he would follow the advice of Mr. Sauvalle, who has technical knowledge.

I understand the minister >
make the statement that Mr. Sauvalle is responsible for the translation of his department as far as the Mines Branch is concerned. Do I understand the minister to state that when Mr. Sauvalle can not do the work-and I do not think there is a man in the world who could do all of this work-he has power to send a document to be translated to a man of his own choice without any further consultation with the



minister? Is that the statement made by the hon. gentleman?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Every time a name is submitted to me of a person said to be qualified for the work of translation, I send it to- Mr. Sauvalle. Mr. Sauval'le tries the man, and if his work is satisfactory he retains hiis services. I am not aware that two new men have been given work since I have been in this department. Mr. Sauvalle has absolute liberty to make a choice amongst those I recommend,, and once more I invite my hon. friend to give me the names of competent men whom they may know.

Any man from L'Ecole Polytechnique could do that work efficiently. As long as my hon. friend takes briefless lawyers to do the work-and he does-he cannot expect them to succeed with what is purely technical work.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is not fair for my hon. friend to make that statement. I never took briefless lawyers.
My hon. friend is responsible for the appointments in his department.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend object with regard to Mr. Daoust?

I do. Mr. Daoust was on the staff of the House of Commons. He was an excellent translator, but my hon. friend put him out and appointed another man, just because Mr. Daoust happened to be a Liberal. Mr. Daoust's place was in the House of Commons where he was doing excellent work. My hon. friend dismissed him and appointed one of his own friends.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Has my hon. friend any proof of that? Does he not know that according to the Civil Service Act a man cannot enter the Service if he is over thirty-five, unless it is for technical work. I did my best for Mr. Daoust and I am still doing so.

I heard the name of
Laframboise mentioned. I see a man by that name in the Auditor General's Report., The initials are not the same, but I should like to know the relationship that exists between the two. This gentleman makes a specialty of ore deposits along the Gatineau river.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I could not give my hon. friend the information, for I do not know these people. As I said to my hon. friend from Rouville, I am willing to submit a

complete list to the House. I am anxious to get the best-men available, and shall be glad to accept any suggestions from hon. gentlemen opposite that would lead to an improvement in the translation of the blue-books.

They say that ignorance is bliss. If that is so, the minister should know what bliss is because he does not know what is going on in his department. It is a poor plea for a minister of the Crown to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It shows that I gave Mr. Sauvalle a free hand ,in selecting the men. The hon. member knows that when it is1 a question of qualifications only, the head of the department is the best judge. Ministers are attacked whenever they depart from that practice.

For a minister of the
ability and reputation of my hon. friend, and occupying the place he does, to try and hide behind the Civil Service Act-well, I think it is a bit too -thin. We know what that means. Does my hon. friend mean to say that there are no translators over thirty-five employed by the department? I know some of them myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I would be in favour of abolishing the thirty-five year limit. I hadi a fight with the Civil Service Commission before they would admit that translation came under section 21. Translators are technical officers.

That was decided long
ago, when I appointed a translator for the Labour Gazette.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: They must have forgotten since.

I wanted to appoint a gentleman by the name of Lanctot as translator for the Labour Gazette. He was over thirty-five, so I applied to the Civil Service Commission. The question whether translation was technical, and should come under section 21, was referred to Sir Allen Ayles-worth, and he decided that translation from English into French, and presumably French into English, was technical work, and came under section 21. So my hon. friend should have no difficulty in getting properly qualified officers appointed in accordance with the Act.
Would the minister, without reading a brief, explain the increase of .$14,000 in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I read the explanation.

Nobody understood it.
Would the minister explain in a few words? Give us the items.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for the compliment he is paying to my English, which I know is not very good.
It is all right.

I was not reflecting on
my hon. friend's English but if his thinking is as clear as mud, it cannot be as clear as crystal.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The Ceramic division
accounts for $6,000. Would my hon. friend like a lecture on the Ceramic division? Then additional equipment for the laboratory at Ottawa accounts for another $6,000. Temporary labour which we have to engage from time to time when experiments are going on, accounts for another $2,000, making a total of $14,000.
What kind of labour is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Day work by labourers. I beg to move that this item of $60,000 for the organization of the exclusive division be reduced to $5,000.

I would like to ask the Secretary of State if tlhere is much printing in connection with this work. As one of the items in this appropriation refers to publication of reports, I thought I might bring the matter up under this heading. There seems to be quite a complaint in the Printing Bureau of some men working overtime while there are a number of printers in the city of Ottawa and in other parts of the Dominion who are walking the streets. There are men in the Printing Bureau who are working above their physical capacity to work; lit is impossible for some of them to work the number of hours for which they are paid, as same of them would have to work twenty-six hours in a day, and there are only twenty-four; so that the wages received by some of those men are absolutely unfair. My hon. friend may know that or he may not, and I do not say that he knows anything about it, but it is the case. There is, for instance, a printer who has earned $101.75 in a fortnight, although his wages are $21 a week.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member discussing the Printing Bureau?

I asked the minister if I could discuss this matter, as there is
147i
an item referring to printing in this Estimate.	.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is not in order in discussing a matter of printing under the Mines Branch. I might point out at the same time that there are items still unvoted in the Printing Bureau.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I shall be very glad to see my hon. friend to-morrow outside of the House and discuss the matter with him.

T have brought this matter up because in this estimate there is an item relating to publication of reports, translation of reports into French, etc. I thought under that heading I could bring this matter up. Of course, if I am out of ordeT, I will not do so, but I thought I might as well bring the matter up now.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: We have been out of order all night, so we might as well continue.
I do not often take up the time of the House, and I am seldom out of order. I do not think it is right of my hon. friend to make that remark.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I was not thinking particularly of my hon. friend. A number ol hon. gentlemen have been out of order.
Am I permitted to proceed ?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Certainly.

I bring this matter to the attention of the minister so that he may look into it and remedy it if possible. There is trouble brewing amongst many of the men working in the Printing Bureau.
I do not want my hon. friend to ask me to give the names, because, if I give the name of any one who furnishes information of any kind, he is liable to be regarded as an informer and to lose his position. I have seen that happen on so many occasions that I do not want to give the names. One man received $81.79 in a fortnight, although he is supposed to have a salary of $21 a week.

Out of curiosity I
would like to . know the name of that individual.	,

The hon. member has
just said that he does not want to mention names.

I do not want to mention names because I know enough of labour. troubles to appreciate what it is to be placed

on the black list when one gives information of any kind. As I have been blackballed myself more than once, I know whereof I speak.
Another man received $96 in two weeks although his salary is $24 a week. There are four men whose salaries are only $15 a week, and in a fortnight one received $65.42, another, $42, another, $47.47, and another, $46.09. If I bring this matter up, it is because there are many printers in the city of Ottawa as well as in other cities throughout the Dominion walking the streets and my hon. friend, if he has not room enough to enlarge his staff, could easily give some of the work he has in hand to outside firms, although I know he is giving a certain amount of work to such firms. It seems to me there is a pact amongst a few men to make a certain amount of money per week regardless of others, and that is absolutely unfair. A few men have control of a certain little ring, and they get men to come whether they work or not and they are paid just the same. Although I do not intend to prove that to-night, I am able to do so. I know even of men who come and sleep all night and who .are paid for it.
You do not want them to sleep in the day time, do you?

It all depends. We often have to do that ourselves when we stay here all night. When a man works all night he has to sleep during the day time. This method of working is creating a good dead of hard feeling and I am bringing this matter up for the good of the department. I know that there has been a delegation, not to my hon. friend, but to his predecessor in office in regard to that matter, and although I appreciate the fact that my hon. friend has recently taken charge of the department, I shall be very glad if he will look into the matter and endeavour to find a remedy.
I will certainly investigate the matter and I shall be very glad to discuss it with my hon. friend at any time.

As I have just come in, I did not know what particular part of the item bias been under discussion. I would like to ask the minister what the proposals are with regard to the last item of this vote, which reads: For practical tests of bitumenous sands of Alberta, for Toadmaking and other purposes, $5,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I understand that we have officers on the spot experimenting, and we are making experiments in the department here on these bitumenous sands. This appropriation is to continue these experiments.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
As my hon. friend has
said, we have experimented in the streets of Edmonton. This item is specially designated for experiments in road building.
Maintenance of assay office, Vancouver, B.C., $25,000.

In the Auditor General's Report of 1914-15, it is shown that the expenditure of the Assay Office in Vancouver, when deductions of $3,259.29 are made, amounted to $15,955.88. This proposed vote of $25,000 is an increase of

$5,000 over last year, and would indicate that the minister intends to expend $9,000 more than he spent in 1914-15.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This assay office is to
help the men who come in from the mines by exchanging their gold for cheques which they can cash at the bank. The reason for the increase this year is that the business has been increasing by leaps and bounds. The following statement will show the increase in five years:
Value of deposits.
1911		$ 641,416
1912		 914,000
1913		   1,448,000
1914		 2,029,000
1915		 2,136,000

But even such an
increase as that would not justify an increase of fifty per cent in the expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The increase in business involves a greater amount of assay work which is costly. In order to cope with the increased business, it is necessary to increase the staff, to purchase more chemical supplies, apparatus, etc., and to have available a large sum to meet miscellaneous expenditures and express charges on the more frequent gold shipments.

But there is no proper
ratio between the increased business that the minister has shown and an increase of fifty per cent in the expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is an increase of only $5,000.
But the expenditure last year was only $16,000, and this proposed vote would authorize an increase of over fifty per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There is a profit made
by this assay office on its operations, which may account for the difference.
That simply strengthens my argument. The ratio of increase in the appropriation is far in excess of the ratio of increase in the number of assays.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The vote of last year was
You did not expend it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes, we spent it, but we are crediting against the $20,000 the profit on bullion to March 13, 1916, $3,105.65. The amount voted last year was $20,000, which has been spent, and the profits are deducted from that amount.

I understand that. This business, although involving an expenditure, is attended also by a certain amount of profit, and that profit depends on the amount of work you are doing. An appropriation of $20,000 was made last year. Either you did not spend that $20,000, or the spending of it brought you a profit of $4,000. This year, if you are going to increase this work, your profits must necessarily increase. If you did not spend the full amount of your appropriation last year, and if the ratio of increase in the work is very small as compared with the ratio of increase in the appropriation, an explanation is surely necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
All I can say is that in these Estimates there is always a certain amount of uncertainty. That we did not spend the whole vote last year is proof of the fact that we spend just what we need.
My officers this year foresee an
11 p.m. expenditure of $25,000. They may not have to spend it all, but they may need that amount. The details of the expenditure for this vote are as follows: salaries of staff, $16,025.
What is the increase over last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I have not under my hand details of the expenditure of last year, but I could get them for my hon. friend. I think the statements made showing the increase of work in this assay office justify the estimate of my officers as to the expenditure for this year.
Geological Survey Branch-for explorations and surveys; ethnological, archEeological and palaeontological investigations; wages of explorers, topographers, draughtsmen and others, $185,000.

I have here the following item from the Ottawa Free Press of Feb. 26:
The Government is doing some real estate business in the Arctic seas. It has sold for $1 per acre some 20 acres of land on Bylot island in Baffin Bay in north latitude 72 degrees, 53 minutes, to the Arctic Gold Exploration Syndicate, Lt., of Torotno.
The land is as yet of course unsurveyed, and the sale is subject to the proviso that the Surveyor-General may later determine the boundaries. *
Apparently the syndicate has found traces of gold in the far north.
Can the minister tell the committee if it is true that a new gold mine has been found in the region referred to, and if it is open to the. public to make application for areas?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Ilf any purchase of land has been made in Baffin bay, it would be through the Interior Department.
Mining land?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Any land. I a-m inclined to think that such a eale has .taken place; if the hon. gentleman wants information he can get it from the Interior Department.
On the other hand, if there is a valuable deposit of 'mineral there, the Geological Survey Deparment would naturally have cognizance of it and would be'in a position to answer the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I do not think there is any question about the matter of a valuable deposit, in so far as we have heard. There wa^ a sale of 20 acres of land, or some small amount like that, in Baffin Bay for a site for certain buildings-not in the sense of there being a valuable mineral deposit.
Mr. 'SINCLAIR: Is gold mining being conducted up there?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Not that I am aware of.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This department has received no communication' in the matter.

During the last session of Parliament I had occasion to draw the attention of the Minister of Mines to reports of important discoveries of metals in Lake Athabasca. An expedition was sent in the spring to make explorations and examination of alleged mineral deposits at the eastern end of Lake Athabasca.
If such an exploration has been made, could the minister inform us how soon the results will be published, and if there is a probability of further research being made in that locality?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The report is now in the printer's hands and will reach my hon. friend very soon.

Could the minister give us any indication of the results of that exploration? Before he replies, I would again call attention to the desirability of securing the earlier publication of the reports of the work of that department. This exploration was made in the early part of last summer, and the report should have been available before now. The delay in the publication of such a report greatly detracts from its value. Before the information becomes available the interest in any alleged discovery is eclipsed by that in the announce-

ment of some new discovery, and so the report fails in its purpose. I would also call attention to the desirability of carrying on exploratory work in connection with petroleum in northern Alberta. On the Athabasca and Peace rivers there are extraordinary evidences of petroleum. Large amounts have been lost by private individuals who have undertaken to bore for petroleum in that country, hitherto without result. Let me suggest that a more thorough examination of the country adjacent to those evidences of petroleum be made by the Geological Survey, with a view to informing- the public in what localities it would be advisable to bore for petroleum. The country is of vast extent, and this course might save further heavy losses. If there is virtue in the science of geology as understood in the Geological Survey Department, surely this is an occasion and, a place foT the application of that scientific knowledge to the most practical purposes. There is to-day a vast and growing demand for petroleum for fuel purposes, We have recently had a discussion in this House on a proposal to impose an increased duty on petroleum for fuel purposes, and large quantities of oil are now being used, in this way on the Pacific coast. The evidences of petroleum of which I speak are immediately east of the mountains. They are in our own country, and are adjacent to the railroads that are now operating with crude oil, and measurably adjacent to the Pacific coast, where the steamers are using crude oil very largely. I would urge upon the Mines Department that the work of their Geological Survey take possibly a more practical turn in the immediate future than it has done in the past, and that the solution of this problem, which is of stupendous economic importance, be given special attention by the department during the coming year. We know there has been an enormous investment in boring for petroleum in southern Alberta, perhaps well advised, perhaps not well advised, but in southern Alberta there is not the enormously widespread evidence of petroleum that there is in northern Alberta. The petroleum'problem in southern Alberta may be too difficult of solution-I am not saying it is-but I say it may easily be. The greatest scientist in the world cannot be expected to know everything below the crust of the earth. But in northern Alberta, where the evidences are so numerous and so plain, there surely is an opportunity for the application of scientific knowledge In
)

demonstrating where it is advantageous to spend money in actually boring for oil and where it is desirable not to spend such money. What I have said in regard to petroleum applies in a somewhat lesser degree to boring for gas. There is gas in that north country. At some places it is in vast quantities and at other places it is not in commercial quantities. I would suggest that along with a closer, more widespread examination for petroleum in that country, there should be an examination and exploration for natural gas. So far as scientific knowledge, under the direction of the minister can be brought to bear, it should be brought to bear in order to reach these practical results which, if reached, would justify all the expenditures which have been made with regard to the Geological Survey. The minister is probably aware that because of the application in a large measure of the energies of the Geological Survey to what might be called academic explorations, there is a question in the minds of many people as to whether the money is well spent. Such explorations as I have suggested, if they resulted either in absolutely establishing that there was not oil, or that there was oil, would well repay the expenditure of the Geological Survey.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I can assure my hon.
friend that it is the intention of the department to proceed along the lines that he has just suggested.

A moment ago, while item 275 was under discussion, my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) asked the minister if it was his intention to continue this year the purchase of specimens for the Victoria Memorial museum. My hon. friend from Pictou read a partial list of the specimens which had been purchased for the museum in 1914-15, as appeared in the last Auditor General's Report which we have before us. He did not exactly complete the list, but he asked a question which remained unanswered. We are on item 277, and as I understand, we are discussing the different sub-items all together. One of these sub-items reads:
For collection and purpose of specimens for the Victoria Memorial Museum, $15,000.
I see that this is practically the amount which was expended in 1914-15, it is the amount which was voted for 1915-16, and the minister is asking for the same amount for 1916-17. At the present time we are occupying the Victoria Memorial Museum as a home for the Parliament of Canada.
It has been magnificently fitted up at very short notice by the Minister of Public Works and it has made for us a very comfortable home. But in order to do this, the department which is now under discussion was obliged to remove from this building and store in the attic or elsewhere the many specimens which had been placed upon exhibition here. It is understood that oui new home on Parliament Hill will not be ready for some time to come. It may take two or three years and at this war time, when we are straining every nerve and every muscle to do all we can for the Empire and for civilization, it appears to me that it is absolutely ridiculous, when the Museum is occupied by Parliament, and there is no place to put specimens, to put a vote in the Estimates to provide for the purchase of $15,000 worth of specimens. I want to know from the minister if it is his intention to buy any more wooden whales with this $15,000. I find that in 1914-15 some of this money was. spent for wooden whales. W. F. Williams of Alberni, B.C., received $10 for a wooden whale and $6 for a mask. That-is not the only thing. The Government paid $247.25 this year for skeletons of buffalo and elk, $200 for a collection of birds, $145 for 32 baskets, $114 for 38 tent mats and $307 for Indian specimens. There are many other items of the same nature in addition to those given by my hon. friend from Pictou. I think it is ridiculous to spend the country's money for specimens, especially when we have no place to put them, and especially in a time like this when we are taxing the publid by direct taxation to pay for the expenses incurred by this war. This item of $15,000, in my humble opinion, and I think in the opinion of hon. members surounding me, should not be placed in the Estimates for the year 1916-17. I therefore beg to move:
That item No. 277 be reduced by $15,000, and that it be $314,400 instead of $329,400.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I may tell my hon.
friend that we did not put this vote in the Estimates with the definite intention of spending it all, or even spending it in part.
Why put it in?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The law which constitutes this department divides it into two branches-the Geological Survey and the Mines Branches. The duty of the officers of the Geological Survey is to maintain a museum of geology and natural history for the purpose of affording complete and exact knowledge on these subjects. I have no

intention of buying here and there everything that may offer without any exercise of judgment. Does the hon. gentleman not think that it is wise to keep a certain amount at the disposal of the officers so that if the opportunity should occur to secure valuable articles for the department they can be purchased?
It might happen that some very valuable specimens were offering cheap, and that it would be in the public interests to buy them. I have in mind no particular object; I cannot foresee just what will be bought. But as a museum has been built, and officers have been appointed to collect specimens, I do not think it would be wise to cut out this item absolutely. I realize, of course, that we have some very interesting specimens in the museum at the present time.
I see mentioned among the specimens, a burial box. Is that for the Minister of Militia and Defence?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I think that was bought about 1911.
Does the minister intend to purchase, and keep in the museum as a souvenir, the old flag that bullet holes were shot through'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I thin* that flag is more the property of my hon. friend, who invented it
Well, will the gentleman who invented it please present it to the museum.
Were the holes in that flag patented?

The minister made a good start by cutting $55,000 out of his Estimates, and I thought he would allow the good impulse to carry him further, and cut out this $15,000 item. According to the press, two ministers of the Crown are going to issue special appeals to the people of this country to economize in their private expenditures. My hon. friend says that he wants this $15,000 item, in case some fellow comes along with a chse of bugs or insects and offers to sell them to the Government for $2,000, like that Yankee did last year. Can my hon. friend imagine a wife when her husband tells her they will have to economize and live on $10,000 instead of $20,000 in the coming year, saying: "Oh, but you must lot me have $15,000; I want $5,000 on hand in case a man comes along with
tj[r, Blondin.]
some curios that I could put in the front parlour." My hon. friend can see how ludicrous that would 'be at a time when economy was very necessary. If .my hon. friends buys any insects or wooden whales, he has no place to put them; he will have to rent a warehouse to lodge them in. Perhaps those gentlemen who came in a few moments ago, in expectation of a vote, would like to hear what this $15,000 is for, and it is well that the country should know how this Government proposes to spend the people's money. One man by the name of Evans got $2,000 for a collection of insects. The Foote Mineral Company of Philadelphia got $3,874 for meteorites, aerolites, sdderites, and uraninites. Another gentleman disposed of an Eskimo birdskin suit to an unsuspecting Government, who 'alleged that they were trying to economize, for $35. Another man by the name of Harris, from London, England, who had a collection of Indian and Esquimaux native articles sold them to the Government for $500. Mr. E. W. Hawkes, of Ottawa, sold some Eskimo specimens, models, one limestone kettle, one walrus tusk .and sundry other specimens to the Government for $675. Then the Government went down to Old Town, Maine, and bought a collection of Micmac Indian relics from G. A. Paul for $175. There were other items, bringing the expenditure up to $15,585. My hon. friend from Shefford (Mr. Boivin) moves that this item be struck out. Why the minister should want this money is - incomprehensible. He cannot possibly house any specimens he buys in this museum. There can be no possible reason for any expenditure under this head, no matter how rare the specimen, until the war is over and normal times have returned.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The only answer I can
give is that the department will not. spend the money except in case of necessity. This vote has always been provided in the past. We have not spent a cent under this head since the -war.
Mr. MACDONALD; You did up to March 31, 1915.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We did not expect the war would last so long. I can assure my hon. friend that if we can possibly avoid it nothing under this head will be expended.
I would not ask that the money be voted if I did not think it was in the interests of the country. I think it would be unwise to cut out the item .altogether.
Why not boil the item down in that limestone kettle that the department bought?

The figures that the hon. member for Pictou and I have quoted from the Auditor General's Report covered expenditures for the year 1914-1915. Part of these expenditures were made before the war, and part after. I should like the minister to tell us how this $15,000 was spent last year. What curios were bought during 1915-16 when the war was on?

I see the department
also bought a messenger pigeon at the price of $25. Was it alive or dead?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have done my best to master the work of my department since I took charge, but I have not yet reached this most interesting branch. That is why I am at a loss to answer all the questions of my hon. friend.
Perhaps that pigeon might replace some of the messengers.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have not the details to answer my hon. friend, but when my Estimates are called again, I will be prepared to give all the details.
Will you bring the pigeon if you can find it?

If we can discuss upon this amendment of mine also the original item, I would like to ask the hon. minister why it is that his department acts in a different manner from other departments, that is, in regard to clothing for the attendants. I see in Estimate No. 277 an item for $54,000, which is $125 less than last year, and in that item, after providing for temporary clerks and other assistance, he provides for clothing for five attendants. Will the minister tell us why he is kind enough to buy clothing for his attendants while the attendants in the other departments have to provide their own clothing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It would be very hard for me to give my hon. friend any other answer than it is the usage in this department.

While this may be an absolutely legitimate expenditure, I think it would be only fair to tell the committee that is being asked to vote this money how it happens that these attendants require this clothing. Is it for some special work in the department which might ruin their clothes that this special clothing has to be provided? I am not saying that it is a
wrong expenditure; I am merely asking for information to which I think the committee is entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The information given me is that the officers who are in special charge of the museum have special clothing because they are called upon to serve the public.
You mean uniform.
If the word "uniform" had been used, we could have understood the expenditure better.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: In the other departments there, are officers in special uniforms, and in this department, as it is a place where visitors come, I suppose the reason for providing uniforms for these men is that they must be well clad, and that they should be dressed differently from the other employees of the building.

I thought this was for clothing used when making special tests. If this item is for uniforms for the guardians or for the officers in charge of the Victoria Memorial Museum, I respectfully request that it should be cut out this year, because there is now no Victoria Memorial Museum to be guarded; it has been transformed into the home of Parliament. We have here as guardians the guardians we had up on Parliament Hill, and I do not know why this vote should go through this year. If the employees are not going to 'work for the Government this year, or if they are going to receive their salaries and remain at home, I think we could dispense with supplying them with uniforms.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is explained that these men are no longer in the department. If they are not employed as they have been in the past, they will not need these special clothes, as they will not have to wear them. We shall therefore not have to expend the money.

The item remains in the Estimates, and I would like to know how much of this $54,000 is devoted to clothing for these special attendants. That is certainly a question to which we are entitled to receive 'an- answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: It is about $450.
I notice there are 21 nests, $28.06. I wonder if it is one of the nests of traitors of 1896.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
It would need to be very large, because there would be many

if I judge them on the gauge that my hon. friend is using.

Might I also ask very seriously an explanation of the last paragraph of estimate No. 277. I see here an item to compensate John F. Lyons for quarters, fuel, light and water supplied him as resident caretaker of the Geological Museum, Sussex street, vacated on removal to the Victoria Memorial Museum, $400. I see that the same $400 was voted last year to compensate the same Mr. John F. Lyons for absolutely the same thing. Are we going to -compensate Mr. John F. Lyons every year for having removed from one building to another?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The information as to
that item is as follows: undet the terms of his appointment as resident caretaker of the Geological Survey, Mr. Lyons was supplied with living quarters, fuel, light and water, and so were his predecessors, both at Montreal and at Ottawa. In the new building, living quarters have not been provided for a resident caretaker. The value of the above was officially estimated at $400 per annum. In addition to his duties as caretaker he has supervision of messengers and labourers, stationery, office supplies, freight and express shipments. This is part of his salary, and as he has been deprived of part of his salary it is only fair that he should be reimbursed.
At what time was he deprived of this portion of his salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: When the department moved from Sussex street, about four or five years ago.

Would it not be very much less trouble to add this $400 to his . salary and let him get -the money in that
way?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
That would be better,
and I really wonder why it was not done before. I will take the advice of my hon. friend and try to have the amount paid in that way.
That would be much better because it would allow the minister to show a reduction of $400 in this item.
The minister has mentioned about Mr. Lyons having supervision of stationery. Is that the stationery supplied to the House of Commons?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Lyons is the caretaker of the Geological Survey.
There is an expenditure on stationery in this item. Does that belong to the Department of the Secretary of State?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This has nothing to do with the Secretary of State.
Amendiment of Mr. Boivin negatived: yeas, 16; nays, 24.
Progress reported.
On the motion of Mr. Rogers, the House adjourned -at 11.56 p.m.
Thursday, March 30, 1916.
